exp.0:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Zechariah in the eighth month of the second year of King Darius. It mentions that Zechariah was the son of Berechiah and the grandson of Iddo. The word "came" in the verse introduces the message that follows.

King Darius ruled the Persian empire. The Jews had returned from exile in Babylon and were living in a land still struck by hardship, with the temple not yet rebuilt. Because of the reference to Darius's reign, this moment is usually placed around the year 520 BC. Zechariah speaks on behalf of God. His message begins by calling the people to return to Him, reminding them that their ancestors had turned away.

Today we can learn that God still speaks and invites us to draw near to Him. If we feel far away, we can pray sincerely, set aside what pulls us apart, and seek Him again, trusting that He responds.
exp.0:1:
The Lord was very angry with the people's ancestors. The phrase "was very angry" is the way the verse expresses how serious his displeasure was, and it is the way Zechariah opens his message.

Zechariah speaks on God's behalf, around the year 520 BC. The Jews had returned from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding the temple. Their fathers had ignored the warnings of the prophets, and that is why they had been taken into exile. God reminds them of that history, but right away he invites them to turn back to him, so that they do not repeat the same mistake.

For today: the past can teach us without condemning us. If we acknowledge our mistakes and those of our family, we can draw near to God with sincerity. He promises to come near to those who turn back to him.
exp.0:3:
God asks the people not to repeat the mistake of their ancestors. The earlier prophets called out to them, so to speak, urging them to abandon their evil ways and their wrongdoing, but they did not listen.

Zechariah speaks to the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon, around 520 B.C. God calls them to learn from history: their fathers ignored the warnings and suffered the consequences. Here God not only corrects, he also invites: if they turn back to him, he will turn back to them.

For today: do not wait until you suffer the consequences to listen to God. If you sense that a warning in his Word touches some habit or attitude of yours, respond to him today with humility, changing course and returning to him.
exp.0:4:
What it says: God asks two questions that answer themselves. The ancestors of that people have already died, and the prophets too. No one lives forever in this world. "Fathers" here means ancestors.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, at the beginning of his ministry, in the second year of King Darius. The people had returned from exile in Babylon. God calls them to turn back to Him and not to repeat the hardness of their ancestors, who ignored the prophets. The prophets died, but their words were fulfilled, as the following verse shows.

For today: Life is brief and people pass away, but the word of God remains. Do not put off turning to Him until tomorrow. Listen to His voice today, and let His word correct your path while you still have time.
exp.0:6:
This verse gives us the date and the name of the prophet. It says that God spoke to Zechariah on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, called Shebat, in the second year of King Darius. The phrase "the word of the Lord came" means that God himself gave him the message. Zechariah is identified as the son of Berechiah and the grandson of Iddo.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and introduces a new word from God. About three months earlier, Zechariah had called the people to return to God. Now a series of night visions begins. According to the Jewish calendar, that month corresponds roughly to February, and the year is usually placed around 519 B.C., although the exact dates are calculated in different ways.

For today: God speaks at specific times and places, and his word is real and trustworthy. Today we can read the Bible with confidence that He still speaks to his people and wants to guide us.
exp.0:7:
Zechariah tells that he had a vision at night. He saw a man riding on a reddish horse, standing among myrtle trees in a low place, or valley. Behind him came other horses: reddish, speckled (with a light coat marked with spots), and white. The next verse makes clear that this man is a messenger of God and that the horses represent those sent to go through the earth.

The prophet Zechariah speaks in the second year of King Darius, when the people had returned from exile and the rebuilding of the temple had stalled. God was calling them to return to Him, and this vision showed them that He remained attentive to what was happening in the world. Scholars interpret the details in various ways.

Even when everything seems still and dark, like a night, God is not absent. Today you can pray with confidence, knowing that He sees your situation and works even when you do not notice it.
exp.0:8:
Zechariah sees a vision at night: a rider standing among myrtle trees, and behind him horses of several colors. Not understanding what they mean, he respectfully asks, "What are these, my lord?" The angel who explains the visions answers that he will show him what they are.

Zechariah speaks as a prophet who writes after the return from exile, in the second year of Darius. The people are discouraged, and the rebuilding is going slowly. God shows him visions to encourage him, and Zechariah does not pretend to understand but asks. The angel commits to giving him the verse, and the verses that follow develop it.

For today: when you do not understand what God allows or shows in his Word, ask him with humility and trust. He often teaches step by step, and sincere doubt does not offend him.
exp.0:9:
The man who stood among the myrtle trees explained who the riders were: they are the ones God sent to go throughout the earth, like messengers who observe what is happening.

Zechariah sees a vision at night, toward the time of the return from exile, when Jerusalem was still in ruins. The man among the myrtle trees appears to be the angel of the Lord, although some understand it in a different way. The riders report that the earth is quiet, but that calm was not good news for a people who were waiting for their restoration. That is why the angel asks God for compassion.

For today: God sees the whole earth and nothing escapes Him. When everything seems silent and nothing changes, we can pray with confidence, knowing that He remains attentive and that our waiting does not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.0:11:
Here the angel of the Lord asks God a question: how long will he go on withholding mercy from Jerusalem and from the cities of Judah? According to the angel, God has been full of wrath against them for seventy years. To show mercy means to show compassion and to restore.

Zechariah receives this vision at night, when the people had already returned from exile, but the temple still had not been rebuilt. The messengers report that the whole earth is at rest, and that contrasts with the condition of Judah. The seventy years are usually understood as the time of punishment, although scholars debate how to count them exactly. God answers with good and comforting words.

For today: when your situation seems stuck, you can bring your questions to God honestly, as the angel does. Praying this way is not a lack of faith; it is trusting that God hears and can answer with comfort.
exp.0:12:
God did not leave the angel's question unanswered. The Lord replied with kind words, that is, gracious messages full of goodness, and with comforting words, words that brought comfort. The angel who was speaking with the prophet was the one who received this answer.

The prophet Zechariah describes a night vision. The angel of the Lord had asked how long God would go on without showing mercy toward Jerusalem, after about seventy years of punishment. God answers with comfort, and then the angel asks Zechariah to proclaim that message: God loves his city with a fierce jealousy and will act.

For today: when you feel weary of waiting, bring your questions to God with sincerity. He can answer with comfort, though not always right away. Trust that his heart toward his people is good.
exp.0:15:
God says that he has returned to Jerusalem with compassion. There his house will be rebuilt, that is, the temple, and the measuring line will be stretched out, which was the cord with a weight that builders used to measure and align. It is the sign that the work of rebuilding the city would truly begin.

Zechariah prophesied after the return from exile in Babylon, when the people were discouraged and the temple still had not been finished. God speaks through an angel and promises to restore what he had allowed to fall because of his people's disobedience. He also becomes angry with the nations that took advantage of the punishment.

For today: if you feel that your life is in ruins, God knows how to return with compassion and rebuild. Trust in him and take the first step of obedience, even if it is small.
exp.0:18:
Zechariah sees four horns and asks the angel what they mean. The angel answers that these are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. Here "scattered" means dispersed with violence, the way wheat is thrown into the air and blown apart. The horn is a symbol of strength and power.

Zechariah speaks with the angel who explains the visions to him. God gives them to the people who returned from exile, discouraged and still surrounded by enemies. The four horns represent powers that oppressed God's people; it is not known with certainty which ones they were, and scholars have proposed different options. The message is that God saw that suffering.

For today: when you feel that something stronger than you has scattered you or discouraged you, remember that God sees your situation and does not ignore it. Bring it to him in prayer with confidence.
exp.0:19:
God showed the prophet Zechariah four carpenters, that is, four craftsmen or smiths who work with tools. The Hebrew word can be understood as workers who labor with wood or metal.

Zechariah speaks after the people returned from exile. He has just seen four horns, which represent nations that scattered Judah. Many think the four do not refer to an exact number of nations, but to a complete enemy power, though this cannot be known for certain. The carpenters come to tear down those horns, and so God comforts a discouraged people.

God sees the harm we suffer and also prepares his response. When you feel that evil has the last word, remember that God is already at work, even though you cannot see it yet.
exp.0:20:
Zechariah asks what the four craftsmen are going to do. The angel explains that the horns, symbols of powerful nations, scattered Judah so thoroughly that no one could lift up their head, meaning they lived humbled. Now the craftsmen come to make them afraid, and to tear down the horns of those nations. To "scatter" means to drive far away, the way grain is blown away from the chaff.

Zechariah speaks with an angel in a vision, after the people returned from exile in Babylon. He was discouraged and still weak. God shows that the powers that oppressed them do not have the final word. Scholars do not agree on identifying the four horns precisely; they may represent empires or the four points of the compass.

For today: when something leaves you with your head bowed, remember that God sees those who oppress you and also has a response. Trust and pray, even if you do not yet see the change.
exp.1:0:
The prophet Zechariah says that he lifted up his eyes and saw a man with a measuring line in his hand. A measuring line was a cord used to calculate the size of a piece of land or of a building. This is one of the visions Zechariah received at night.

The speaker is Zechariah, who writes after the people of Judah returned from exile in Babylon. Jerusalem was weak and without walls. In the verses that follow, we see that the man is going to measure the city. Some understand that the measuring points to its rebuilding; others also see a promise of future growth. Who that man is, is not stated clearly.

God knows your plans and your ruins, and still has purposes for them. When something in your life seems destroyed, pray with hope: God knows how to measure and to raise up again what seemed lost.
exp.1:1:
Zechariah asks the man with the measuring line, "Where are you going?" He answers that he is going to measure Jerusalem, to see how wide it is and how long it is.

Zechariah speaks of a night vision. The people had returned from exile in Babylon, and the city lay in ruins. Measuring a city is often a step toward rebuilding it or marking its boundaries. But soon an angel makes clear that Jerusalem will have no walls, because it will be so large that walls could not contain it, and God will protect it (v. 5). Some see here a promise for the near future; others, something broader and more spiritual.

For today: do not put small limits on what God can do. When your situation looks like ruins, trust that He cares for it and makes it grow beyond what you can measure.
exp.1:4:
It says that God himself will be like a wall of fire around Jerusalem, that is, a protection no one can break through. Furthermore, God will be in the midst of the city, and his presence will be his glory.

The Lord speaks through an angel, in a vision given to the prophet Zechariah. Jerusalem was being rebuilt after the exile, and the city would grow so much that it could not be contained within walls. God promises that it will not need walls of stone, because he himself will watch over it. Some see here a promise for Jerusalem of that time, and others also a foretaste of the future of God's people.

Today we can trust that God's protection is more certain than any human defense. When you feel fear or a lack of security, remember that he is with you, and seek to live close to his presence.
exp.1:8:
He says that God will raise his hand against the nations that mistreated his people. Raising the hand is a gesture of power and judgment. Those nations will become plunder for their own servants: what they took by looting will be seized by those who once served them. When this happens, they will know that the Lord of hosts sent the one who speaks.

Zechariah lives after the return from exile in Babylon. In this vision, the one who speaks has been sent by God, and many Christian believers see here the Messiah, though others interpret it differently. God encourages his people, for whoever touches them touches the apple of his eye, that is, what he cares for most.

For today: when you feel small or mistreated, remember that God watches over you closely. Trust him and leave justice in his hands.
exp.2:3:
The angel of the LORD here commands those standing before him to take away Joshua the high priest's filthy clothes. He then tells him that his iniquity has been removed from him, and that he now clothes him with fine garments, that is, rich clothing fit for a festive occasion.

Zechariah saw this scene in a vision, after the people returned from exile. Joshua represents the people and their priestly service. Satan was accusing him, but the LORD rebuked him and rescued him like a brand plucked out of the fire. Many Christians see here an image of the forgiveness God gives through his grace.

For today: if God has forgiven you, do not live under shame or accusations. Receive his forgiveness with gratitude and walk in the new life he gives you.
exp.2:4:
Here someone gives the order to place a clean turban on the head of Joshua, the high priest. So they do it, and they also dress him in new clothes. The verse says they set a fair mitre on his head and clothed him with garments, and while this happens, the angel of the Lord stands by, directing and approving everything.

Joshua was standing before the angel in filthy clothes, a sign of his sin and that of his people. The angel ordered that they be taken off and declared that his guilt had been removed. This vision encouraged the people who were returning from exile: God was forgiving them and restoring them to serve him. Some believe it also points to the Messiah.

For today: God not only forgives, he also restores you and gives back your dignity. If you carry guilt for something you have already handed over to him, receive his forgiveness and live with gratitude and obedience.
exp.2:5:
The verse says that the angel of the Lord spoke to Joshua, which means he addressed him solemnly, like someone giving a warning or a serious charge. Today we would say he declared to him firmly, or warned him with conviction, what follows.

Joshua, the high priest, has just been stripped of his filthy clothes and dressed in festive garments and a clean turban. This shows that God removed his guilt. Now the angel, who speaks with God's authority, explains that this forgiveness brings a responsibility: to walk in obedience and to serve in the house of God.

God forgives us by sheer grace, but that forgiveness is not meant to leave us unchanged. It is the beginning of a new life. Ask God today for help to live faithfully in what He has entrusted to you.
exp.2:8:
God says that he set a stone before Joshua, the high priest. That stone has seven eyes, and God himself will engrave it. The engraving means what is cut or carved into the stone. Also, God promises to remove the sin of the land in one day.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah to the people who had returned from exile. Joshua had been shown in dirty clothes, and then he was forgiven and cleansed. Before this verse, God announces his servant, the Branch. The stone and the seven eyes are understood in several ways: many see the Messiah there, and the seven eyes as God's complete sight or care, but not everyone agrees.

For today: trust that God is the one who removes sin, not your own efforts. If you feel unclean because of your failures, come near to him and receive his forgiveness.
exp.3:1:
Here the angel asks Zechariah what he sees, and he describes a vision: a lampstand made entirely of gold. On top of it is a bowl, which is a container for the oil. It has seven lamps and seven channels or pipes that carry the oil to them.

Zechariah was a prophet after the return from exile in Babylon. The people were rebuilding the temple and felt weak and discouraged. The angel had roused him, as if from sleep, to show him this vision. Shortly afterward, the message becomes clear: the work would be done not by human strength, but by the Spirit of God (4:6). The oil is usually understood as an image of that Spirit, though the meaning of each symbol is debated.

Today, when your task seems greater than your strength, remember that the light does not depend on your effort, but on the oil that God provides. Ask him for his help every day.
exp.3:2:
It says that, beside the golden lampstand Zechariah saw, there were two olive trees: one on the right side of the bowl that holds the oil, and the other on its left side. "Olive trees" are the trees themselves, and the bowl is the container where the oil was kept for the lamps.

Zechariah tells of a vision that an angel shows him at night. God was encouraging the people who had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, with little human power. Later in the chapter, the olive trees are connected with two anointed ones, and many think these refer to Zerubbabel and Joshua, though some interpret them in other ways. The central point is that the oil, a symbol of the Spirit, sustains the light (4:6).

For today: do not depend only on your own strength. Ask God for his Spirit each day so that you can serve with patience, knowing that he keeps alive the light he entrusted to you.
exp.3:5:
It says that God sends a message to Zerubbabel: the work will not be accomplished by an army or by human strength, but by the Spirit of the LORD.

Zechariah has a vision of the golden lampstand and the olive trees, and he does not understand what it means. The angel explains it with this message. Zerubbabel was the governor of Judah who led the rebuilding of the temple after the exile. The people were few, tired, and facing opposition. Many understand that the "spirit" here refers to the Spirit of God at work, although the text gives no further detail.

When you face a task that is beyond you, do your part with effort, but do not rely only on your own abilities. Pray, ask God for direction, and rest in the knowledge that his Spirit can do what you cannot.
exp.3:7:
This verse is a short phrase that introduces what follows. It says that the word of God came to Zechariah once more. The sentence that explains the old spelling of a word has been removed, since that spelling does not appear in your verse.

The speaker is Zechariah, a prophet who lived after the return from exile in Babylon. The people were rebuilding the temple and felt weak and small. God had already said that the work would not be done "by might, nor by power, but by my spirit." Now Zechariah receives a new word to confirm that Zerubbabel would finish what he had begun.

For today: when a task seems too large, do not lose heart. God often speaks and sustains those who obey him, even when the beginning is small. Listen to his word and take the next step with confidence.
exp.3:8:
Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, laid the foundation of the temple, and he himself will finish it. The house is the temple in Jerusalem. The Lord of hosts is God, who rules over all power. When the work is completed, the people will recognize that God sent the messenger.

A messenger from God, an angel, speaks to the prophet Zechariah. The Jewish people had returned from exile in Babylon, but the rebuilding had stopped because of opposition and discouragement. The work seemed small and weak. God promises that what was begun will be completed, not by human strength, but by his Spirit (v. 6).

For today: if God has led you to begin something good, do not lose heart because its progress is slow or it looks small. Remain faithful, trusting that God is the one who gives the fruit and brings it to completion.
exp.3:9:
They who despised the small beginning of the work will rejoice when they see the plumb line, a mason's tool for checking that a wall stands straight, in the hand of Zerubbabel. That shows the building is moving forward and will be finished. The "seven" mentioned are the eyes of the Lord, which run to and fro through the whole earth. Many understand this to mean that God sees and watches over everything.

The angel speaks to the prophet Zechariah, and God encourages Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah. The Jews had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, but the work seemed small and weak compared with the earlier temple. God promises that Zerubbabel began it and will finish it.

For today: do not despise small beginnings, either in your own life or in the lives of others. If God has given you a humble task, continue faithfully, because He watches over the work and knows how to bring it to completion.
exp.4:1:
Here the prophet Zechariah recounts a vision. An angel asks him what he sees, and he answers that he sees a scroll, that is, a rolled-up parchment with writing on it, flying through the air. It is twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide. A cubit is roughly half a meter, so that would be about ten meters by five.

Zechariah prophesied to the people of Judah, who had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. He speaks with the angel who explains the visions. The scroll represents God's curse against theft and false oaths. Many note that its size matches that of the holy place of the tabernacle, though not everyone interprets this the same way. Its message is that God's law applies to everyone.

For today: God takes honesty seriously. Check whether there is something you should give back or a promise you should keep, and ask God for forgiveness and help to live with integrity.
exp.4:7:
Here the angel explains the vision to Zechariah: the woman sitting inside the ephah (a large basket used to measure grain) represents wickedness. The angel pushes her back down inside and covers the mouth of the ephah with the heavy lead weight, so that she cannot get out.

Zechariah receives this vision at night, during the time of rebuilding after the exile. The angel is showing him that God will remove sin from the community. The ephah points to dishonesty in business, though some scholars see a broader meaning of sin in general. What follows, with two women carrying the ephah far away, shows that God takes wickedness away from his people.

For today: do not downplay sin or let it grow in secret. Ask God to cleanse you, and remove dishonest practices from your life, even when they seem small.
exp.4:8:
Zechariah sees two women flying with the wind in their wings, wings like those of a stork. They lift up the ephah, which was a large basket used for measuring grain, and carry it through the air, between the earth and the heaven. Inside sits the woman named wickedness.

This is part of a series of visions God gave to Zechariah after the return from exile. The angel explains that wickedness is taken out of the land and carried to Shinar, the ancient name for Babylon. Scholars interpret in various ways who the winged women are, but the central message is that God wants to cleanse his people.

For today: God does not only forgive; he also wants to remove evil from our lives. You can ask him to show you something you need to leave behind, and entrust that process to him.
exp.5:0:
Zechariah tells us that he turned, lifted up his eyes, and saw four chariots coming out from between two mountains. Those mountains were made of metal, probably bronze.

This verse closes the series of eight night visions that God gave to Zechariah, a prophet who encouraged the people who had returned from exile to Jerusalem. Zechariah is the one speaking, and an angel explains what he sees. The chariots seem to represent God's action throughout the earth, and the mountains of metal suggest firmness and protection. Interpreters disagree about the exact meaning of the mountains.

For today: even when the world seems disordered, God continues to rule with firmness. Today you can bring your worries to Him in prayer and trust that He is at work, even when you cannot see it.
exp.5:1:
Zechariah sees a chariot pulled by red horses, that is, reddish in color, and another with black horses. They are part of a vision of four chariots that come out from between two mountains of metal, probably bronze.

Zechariah, the prophet, tells what God shows him at night, when the people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. Later, the angel explains that these chariots are spirits of heaven that go out from the presence of the Lord of all the earth. The exact meaning of the colors is not made clear in the text, and scholars interpret them in several ways. What is clear is that they are sent by God.

For today: even when the world seems confused or out of control, God still governs. Today you can hand over a situation that worries you and trust that he acts with authority and purpose.
exp.5:2:
This verse continues the description of the four chariots that Zechariah sees. Here appear the third, with white horses, and the fourth, with spotted and dappled gray horses. That expression is difficult: the first word refers to horses with patchy, spotted coats, and the second describes a gray with round spots. Other versions translate it as spotted or streaked.

Zechariah recounts a vision he received at night. The chariots come out from between two mountains of bronze, and the angel explains that they are the four winds, or spirits, sent out before the Lord of all the earth. Scholars do not agree on what the colors mean; what is clear is that God sends his messengers with purpose.

For today: even when the world seems turbulent, God still governs. You can rest in the knowledge that nothing escapes him, and pray with confidence.
exp.5:3:
Zechariah sees four chariots with horses of different colors, and he asks the angel who is explaining the vision, "What are these, my lord?"

The prophet Zechariah is speaking; he is seeing one of his visions at night. He does not understand the meaning of the chariots, so he asks respectfully. The angel answers that they are messengers going out from the presence of God, the Lord of all the earth. Scholars interpret the details of these chariots in several different ways.

For today: when something in the Bible or in your life is hard to understand, ask God with humility and sincerity. Asking is not a lack of faith; it is seeking to understand with a heart ready to learn.
exp.5:5:
Here we see a chariot with black horses going out toward the north country. The white horses go out after them, and the grisled horses go out toward the south country.

Zechariah recounts a vision he received at night. The angel explains to him that these chariots represent the four winds, or spirits of heaven, sent out by the Lord of all the earth. Interpreters do not agree on the meaning of the colors. But verse 8 suggests that the north, from where Israel's enemies came, receives the action of God. In this way the people, who were rebuilding the temple, were encouraged.

For today: God governs every place and every situation, even those that seem out of control to you. You can pray and work with calm, trusting that he has the final word.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that the angel, after sending out the chariots, called to the prophet to tell him that the chariots with black horses, the ones that went toward the north, gave rest to God's spirit there. The word for "north" in this passage means the north. The phrase about making God's spirit rest means that they calmed God's anger, or that He was satisfied.

Zechariah sees a vision of four chariots that travel through the earth at God's command. The one speaking is the angel, with the voice of God. The north, from where Babylon had come, was a place of judgment on the nations that had oppressed Israel. Interpreters explain the colors and the chariots in several ways, but the central message is that God governs the nations and His justice is carried out.

For today: when you see injustice that seems to have no end, trust that God still governs. He sees, He acts in His own time, and He can give rest to those who wait for Him.
exp.5:13:
Four men will be remembered, because the crowns will be kept in the temple of the Lord as a memorial, that is, a reminder. Helem seems to be another name for Heldai (v. 10), and Hen could be another name for Josiah, son of Zephaniah, though this is not known for certain.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile. These men brought silver and gold from Babylon, and the crowns were made from it. The gesture pointed ahead to the Branch, a king and priest who would build the temple. Christians see in him Jesus; others connect him with Zerubbabel.

For today: God does not forget simple gifts made in faith. Serve and give generously, even when no one sees you; what you do for Him is kept in His memory.
exp.6:0:
This verse gives the date when God spoke to the prophet Zechariah. It was in the fourth year of King Darius, on the fourth day of the ninth month, called Chisleu.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking here, presenting a new message from God. Darius ruled over Persia, and the Jews had already returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. According to the verses that follow, some men ask whether they should keep the fasts of mourning. God will answer about what truly matters to him.

For today: before repeating a religious custom, ask yourself why you do it. God looks at the heart, and he desires obedience, justice, and mercy, not just rituals.
exp.6:1:
This verse tells that some men were sent to the house of God, the temple in Jerusalem, to seek the favor of the LORD, that is, to seek his goodness and his help through prayer. The names Sherezer and Regem-melech appear here; scholars discuss whether they came from Babylon or were from Bethel, since the Hebrew text allows both readings. That doubt does not change the message.

We are in the fourth year of King Darius, around 518 B.C. The people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple. The envoys arrive with a question about fasting and weeping each year over the destruction of the temple. God answers through Zechariah.

For today: when we seek God, it is good to ask ourselves whether we do so from the heart or only out of habit. God does not look for repeated rituals, but for a life that truly honors him.
exp.6:2:
This verse tells how a delegation went to ask the priests and the prophets of the house of the Lord whether they should keep weeping and fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for so many years.

The people asking are Sharezer and Regem-melech with their men, sent from Bethel, according to the Hebrew text, although some translations render it differently. We are in the year 518 BC. The people remembered with fasting the destruction of the temple, which happened in the fifth month. Now the temple was being rebuilt, and they wondered whether that fasting still made sense. God will answer that He wants sincere hearts, not only rituals.

For today: examine why you do your spiritual practices. Praying, fasting, or going to church has value when it comes from love for God, not from habit or the desire to fulfill an obligation.
exp.6:4:
God tells the prophet to speak to all the people of the land and to the priests. He asks them a pointed question: for seventy years they fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months, but did they really do it for God?

God speaks through Zechariah. A delegation had asked whether they should keep fasting in the fifth month, in memory of the destruction of the temple. God does not answer with a rule but examines the heart. Scholars understand the seventy years as the time of exile and after, although the exact calculations are debated.

For today: examine your religious habits. Fasting, praying, or going to church is not worth anything just because it is customary. Ask yourself honestly: am I doing it for God, or to fulfill an obligation and look good?
exp.6:5:
He says that when the people ate and drank, they did it only for their own pleasure, not for God. It is a question God asks to draw attention. The question presses on them: were you really doing this for yourselves alone?

God speaks through Zechariah. Some men from Bethel had asked whether they should keep fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for about seventy years, remembering the destruction of Jerusalem. God asks them whether those fasts were really for Him. He shows that both the fasting and the feasts had become routine, without a sincere heart.

For today: examine why you do what you do in your life of faith. Before you pray, fast, serve, or even eat, ask yourself whether you are doing it with gratitude toward God, or only out of habit or for yourself.
exp.6:8:
It says that God, the Lord of hosts, asks for true justice: to judge with integrity, without favoritism. He also asks for mercy and compassion, that is, kindness and tenderness, which each person should show to his brother, meaning his neighbor within the people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. Some men had asked him whether they should keep fasting (chapter 7). God answers that what matters is not the ritual, but living with justice and compassion. He reminds them that he had already said this through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was living in peace. The people did not want to listen then.

For today: before doing something religious, let us ask ourselves how we treat people. Today you can help someone in need, or be fair and kind in a disagreement, without taking advantage of anyone.
exp.6:9:
God asks his people not to abuse or oppress others. The verse names four vulnerable people: the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, and the poor. It also warns against thinking evil in the heart, that is, planning harm against a brother even when no one sees it.

The Lord spoke through the prophet Zechariah after the return from exile in Babylon. Some of the people were asking about fasting, and God answers that what matters is justice and mercy. The verses that follow show that their ancestors would not listen, and for that reason punishment came.

For today: look at who around you has less power or voice, such as a migrant, a lonely elderly person, or someone without money. Help them with something concrete, and examine your own thoughts, so that you do not hold on to resentment or contempt.
exp.6:11:
The verse says that the people made their hearts as hard as adamant, that is, a stone so hard nothing can pierce it. They would not hear the law or the messages that God sent them by his Spirit through the earlier prophets. Because of this, a great punishment came from God.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah to a people who had returned from exile in Babylon. He reminds them that their ancestors did not obey, not even in basic matters such as caring for the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor. Their hardness brought the exile. It is a warning not to repeat that history.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, let us not become defensive. Let us ask him for a soft heart and put into practice what we hear, helping someone in need this week.
exp.6:13:
God says that he scattered his people like a whirlwind among nations they did not know. Their land was left so empty that no one went in or out of it. The phrase about the land being left in ruins and emptied of people means it was wrecked and depopulated. Destruction is what the wording points to. The pleasant land is the land of Israel, which was precious and good.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah, a few years after the return from exile in Babylon. He reminds them why their ancestors were punished: they hardened their hearts and would not listen to the prophets. God uses that history as a warning so the new generation does not repeat the same mistake.

For today: let us not wait to suffer the consequences before we listen to God. If you feel that his Word confronts you about something today, answer it with humility and obedience, before your heart grows hard.
exp.7:0:
This verse is an opening phrase. It says that the word of the LORD of Hosts came to Zechariah. The word "again" marks this as one more message in a series. "The LORD of Hosts" is a title of God that stresses his power over all that has been created.

The one speaking is God, and he does so through the prophet Zechariah. This verse introduces a new message, which in the verses that follow speaks of his love for Zion and his promise to dwell in Jerusalem. Zechariah prophesied after the return from exile, when the people were rebuilding and needed encouragement. Scholars do not agree on every detail of the date, but the general sense is clear.

God does not leave his people without a word. Today we can approach the Bible expecting that God wants to speak to us, and listen to him before we worry about everything else.
exp.7:2:
God says that he has returned to Zion, that is, to Jerusalem, and that he will live in the midst of it. The city will be called "the city of truth," and the mountain of the temple, "the holy mountain."

The verse of this verse is that God's return to Jerusalem means that he will live among his people again.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. The city was still fragile and the temple was being rebuilt. God reminds them that his love for Jerusalem is intense, and he promises his presence and a renewed life, which the following verses describe with old men and children in the streets.

For today: God wants to live in the midst of his people, and his presence calls us to truth and holiness. You might ask yourself: in what area of my home or work do I need to be more sincere today, so that God is honored there?
exp.7:3:
It says that in Jerusalem old men and old women will again sit in the public squares, each one with a staff in hand because of the many years they have lived.

The LORD of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile in Babylon. The city was weak and only half rebuilt, and the people were discouraged. God promises that He will again dwell in Jerusalem and that there will be peace and ordinary life there. Elderly people sitting safely in the squares and children playing in the streets show a peaceful city, where people live long and are protected.

For today: God keeps His promises even when what we see seems small or difficult. We can trust Him and take care of our elders and our children, valuing the simple peace of each day.
exp.7:8:
God tells the Jewish people who had returned from exile: "Be encouraged, take heart, let your hands be strong." He is speaking to those who were hearing the words of the prophets from the day the foundation of the temple was laid.

The phrase "let your hands be strong" means: take courage and keep working.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people had returned to Jerusalem, but the rebuilding of the temple had stopped because of fear, opposition, and weariness. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah were encouraging them to resume the work. God reminds them that He wants to save them and to live among them.

For today: if you are tired or discouraged in something God has entrusted to you, remember His promises, ask Him for strength, and take the next step, even if it is a small one.
exp.7:12:
God tells Judah and Israel that they had once been a "curse among the nations," that is, an example of punishment and disaster that other peoples would mention. Now he promises to save them so that they will be a blessing. He asks them not to be afraid and to let their hands be strong, meaning that they should work with courage and determination.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile in Babylon. The people were rebuilding the temple and had become discouraged. God reminds them that just as he carried out his warning of judgment, he will now carry out his promise of good. Scholars debate how this is fulfilled in detail, but the central message is clear.

For today: if you feel that your past or your failures define you, remember that God can change your story. Pray with confidence, let go of fear, and take one concrete step today in the task he has given you, even if it is small.
exp.7:16:
It says that God does not want us to think evil of our neighbor in our hearts, nor to take pleasure in false oaths, that is, swearing lies or giving deceptive testimony. The word the verse uses for "hate" here means that God strongly rejects those things. Wrongdoing begins inside, not only in what is done.

The prophet Zechariah speaks for the LORD after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. God promises good things for Jerusalem and tells the people how to live: to speak truth and to judge with justice at the gates, where legal cases were settled. Many scholars see here that God wants a people renewed in their inner life, not only in their outward conduct.

For today: before letting a suspicion or a grudge grow against someone, bring it before God and ask him for a clean heart. Then make an effort to always speak the truth, even in small things.
exp.8:0:
This verse opens a prophecy against a territory called Hadrach and against Damascus, a city in Syria. The word "burden" means a heavy message, an announcement of judgment. "Its resting place" means the place where that word settles or comes to rest. It says that the eyes of all men and of the tribes of Israel are turned toward the Lord. This last phrase can be understood in several ways, and scholars do not fully agree.

The message comes from God himself, given to the prophet Zechariah after the return from exile. Hadrach is a little-known place, and it is not known with certainty where it was. God shows that he rules over the neighboring nations of his people.

Today we can remember that no human power escapes the gaze of God. When you see injustice or fear around you, fix your eyes on him, because he is still in control.
exp.8:1:
This verse continues the announcement of judgment against several cities neighboring Israel. It says that Hamath, a city to the north, will also be under this message, and so will Tyre and Sidon, coastal cities known for their wisdom and skill, though very wise they may be. The phrase about Hamath having its boundary there is understood in several ways; it probably means that Hamath borders that land and shares its fate.

The prophet Zechariah speaks, bringing the word of the LORD. God declares that no nation, however strong or clever it may be, escapes his rule. The verses that follow show that Tyre trusted in its strength and its riches.

For today: intelligence, money, and the security we achieve are valuable gifts, but they should not be our final refuge. We can use well what we have and, at the same time, place our trust in God.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the city of Tyre built itself a stronghold and piled up so much silver that it looked like dust, and so much gold that it looked like the mud of the streets. The word "heaped up" means it gathered them in great quantities. It is a way of saying that Tyre was extremely rich and felt secure.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, in a message against the neighboring cities of Israel. Tyre was a famous trading port, and its wealth and its defenses gave it confidence. But the verses that follow announce that the Lord will strip it of its riches and strike down its power at sea. Scholars often connect this with the conquest of Alexander the Great, though some interpret it in other ways.

For today: the money and security we build cannot protect us from everything. We can work and save wisely, but our firmest trust must be in God, not in what we have.
exp.8:3:
It says that God will take away all of Tyre's riches. God will bring it down there, and in the end the city will be consumed by fire, that is, completely destroyed.

The prophet Zechariah speaks on God's behalf. Tyre was a rich and proud city, built on an island, that trusted in its wisdom, its silver, and its walls. The passage announces that God judges the neighboring nations of Israel. Many believe this was partly fulfilled through the conquest of Alexander the Great, though not everyone interprets it the same way.

For today: do not put your security in money, in your achievements, or in your intelligence. All of that can disappear. Rather, trust in God, who sustains your life and cares for you.
exp.8:4:
The Philistine cities of Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron will see the fall of Tyre and feel fear and great sorrow. They had hoped that Tyre would protect them, but their hope will be shamed. Gaza will lose its king, and Ashkelon will be left without inhabitants.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Zechariah. This passage announces judgment on cities neighboring Israel, which trusted in their strength and their riches. Many scholars connect it with military campaigns in the region, sometimes with Alexander the Great, though not all agree. The following text shows that God also promises mercy to some of these peoples.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our hope: in money, in positions, or in powerful people. All of these can fail. Trusting in God gives us a security that does not collapse.
exp.8:5:
It says that in Ashdod, a Philistine city, a foreigner will live, and that God himself will bring an end to the pride of the Philistines. "Cut off" means to bring down or cut off, as one cuts down a tree. "Pride" is haughtiness and arrogance. The Philistines are the people who lived next to Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He announces his judgment on the Philistine cities, which trusted in their strength and wealth. Scholars debate when and how this was fulfilled, but the meaning is clear: God rules over the nations. What follows also shows his mercy, for some of them will belong to our God, and he will care for his house.

For today: pride and trust in our own strength are fragile. Today you can entrust to God what you trust in most and ask him for humility to depend on him.
exp.8:7:
He says that God himself will be like a camp or a guard of soldiers around his house, that is, his people and his temple. The phrase that was rendered as a military encampment refers to a camp of soldiers. No one who goes or comes will be able to oppress them again, because God says that he has now seen them with his own eyes. The word that was rendered as an oppressor refers to a cruel oppressor or tax collector.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. Earlier he announced judgment on the neighboring nations, such as the Philistines, and that some of them would be joined to his people. Here he promises protection to Israel. Then comes the announcement of the humble king riding on a donkey, which Christians connect with Jesus. Some scholars think the protection first referred to the time after the exile, and others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: when you feel vulnerable or pressured, remember that God sees you and cares for you. Rest in his protection and pray with confidence.
exp.8:8:
This verse is an invitation to celebrate with joy. God tells Jerusalem, called the daughter of Zion, to rejoice and shout with gladness because her king is coming to her. That king is just, brings salvation, and is humble. He does not come on a war horse but on a donkey, that is, on a young donkey, a colt.

Zechariah is a prophet who speaks after the return from exile. In the verses before this one, God promises to protect his people from their enemies. Here he announces a different king: his power is not based on violence, and it is then said that he will cut off the chariot and the war bow and speak peace to the nations. The Gospels quote this passage when Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a donkey (Matthew 21:4-5).

Today we can learn that Jesus reigns with humility and peace. If we follow him, we too can treat others with gentleness, without pride or harshness.
exp.8:9:
He says that God will take away the weapons of war: the chariots of Ephraim, the horses of Jerusalem, and the bows used in battle. Instead of violence, the king who is coming will proclaim peace to the nations. His rule will reach from one sea to the other, that is, very far, and from the river (probably the Euphrates) to the ends of the earth. The word "dominion" means royal authority.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Zechariah, to a people who were suffering and waiting for deliverance. Just before this, he announces a humble king riding on a donkey. The New Testament connects this image with Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:4-5). Some believe the full fulfillment of world peace is still to come.

For today: trust that Jesus reigns in a different way, with humility and peace. When you feel tempted to respond harshly or to rely on your own strength, ask him to teach you to be a peacemaker.
exp.8:10:
God tells his people that they will be saved by the blood of his covenant, that is, by the agreement he made with them, which was sealed with blood. He also says that he has brought out the prisoners from the cistern, a dry well that served as a water storage pit and sometimes as a prison, where there is no water and no hope.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. It comes after the promise of a humble, righteous and saving king, who rides on a donkey and brings peace. Christians often see Jesus here, and the New Testament connects his blood with the new covenant. God promises to free a captive people and give them hope.

For today: if you feel trapped in a dry well, through guilt, fear or sadness, remember that God knows how to bring out the prisoners. Trust in his covenant and return to him with hope. Ask him today to lift you up.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that the tribe of Ephraim, which represents the northern kingdom of Israel, will be strong like a warrior. Their hearts will be as joyful as when someone enjoys wine. Their children will also see that victory and be glad. All of them will rejoice in the Lord, that is, in the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile. He promises to strengthen Judah and Joseph (Ephraim), to restore his people and to have compassion on them. Some believe it is a promise for his own time, and others also see a future fulfillment. This is debated.

For today: God can restore strength and joy to someone who feels defeated or far away. That joy does not depend on circumstances, but on trusting in Him. Today you can thank Him for His faithfulness, and tell your children or those around you what God has done in your life.
exp.9:7:
God says he will call his people with a whistle, the way a shepherd or beekeeper calls his own to gather them. He will bring them together because he has already redeemed them, that is, rescued them and made them his own. And their number will grow again, as it did in the past.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the exile. He promises to strengthen Judah and Joseph (the northern kingdom, Ephraim), and to restore the whole people. The verses that follow mention Egypt and Assyria as places of scattering. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile; others see one still to come.

For today: if you feel far away or scattered, remember that God knows you and calls you. His love does not depend on your past, but on what he has already done for you. Respond to his call.
exp.9:10:
He says God will open a way for his people, even through the sea. The distress, or anguish, will cross the waters and strike them, and even the deepest part of the river will be dried up. The proud power of Assyria will be brought down; the might of Egypt will disappear. In other words, nothing will be able to stop the return of those who were carried away into exile.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the exile. Assyria and Egypt stand for the places from which the people were scattered and oppressed. Some think the sea refers to the Red Sea and the Exodus; others take it as a general image. God promises to gather and restore his people.

For today: when you feel that something greater than you is blocking your path, remember that God knows how to open ways. Trust that his power is greater than any human pride, and take the next step with faith.
exp.10:0:
It says that Lebanon, famous for its tall cedars, must open its gates so that fire may enter and consume them. It is a poetic image: a strong forest is spoken of as being destroyed.

Zechariah speaks as a prophet of God, and the language is that of judgment. The cedars, the oaks of Bashan, and the proud thickets of the Jordan represent powerful and proud people, such as leaders or nations. The shepherds who wail would be those rulers who mourn their loss. Interpreters differ: some think of the fall of Jerusalem or its temple, others of judgment on the neighboring nations. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: nothing that makes us feel great, such as money, success, or prestige, is as firm as God. Today you can ask Him to help you live with humility and to trust in Him, not in your own strength.
exp.10:1:
Here the trees are called on to wail aloud. The word for wailing means crying out loudly, with pain. The fir tree (or cypress, according to other translations) must lament because the cedar, the tallest and noblest tree, has already fallen. The oaks are the sturdy trees of Bashan, and that region was famous for its forests. The dense forest, now brought down, is the thick woodland that has fallen.

The prophet Zechariah speaks here, announcing judgment on behalf of God. The trees probably represent the leaders and powerful people of the nation, as the shepherds who weep afterward suggest. Interpreters differ about which historical event is in view: some think of the destruction of Jerusalem, others of a wider judgment.

For today: let us not trust in power, fame, or wealth, for even what stands highest can fall. Let us place our security in God, who remains firm, and live with humility.
exp.10:7:
This verse says that the shepherd, who speaks on behalf of God, removed three shepherds or leaders of the people within a single month. It also says that he grieved over them, and that they came to loathe him.

Zechariah acts as a symbolic shepherd sent to a flock mistreated by corrupt leaders. Who the three shepherds are is not known with certainty; some have proposed kings, priests or prophets, and others see a symbolic expression. What is clear is that the flock and its guides reject the good shepherd.

For today: when someone cares for others and corrects them with love, they sometimes receive rejection. Even so, we should not stop seeking the good of others, and we should humbly examine whether we ourselves receive correction.
exp.10:14:
God tells the prophet to take up again the tools of a shepherd, but now those of a foolish shepherd, that is, one without wisdom or care. The verse speaks of a flock of sheep. This is a symbolic action: the prophet is to represent a bad shepherd.

The Lord speaks and gives the command to the prophet Zechariah. Earlier, the prophet had represented the good shepherd, but the people rejected him and put a price on him of thirty pieces of silver. Now God shows what happens when a people rejects the good shepherd: leaders arrive who take advantage of the sheep. The verses that follow explain this. Some Christians see here a reference to Christ, since the Gospels mention the thirty pieces of silver.

For today: value the leaders who serve and care, and examine whom you follow. If you are a leader, remember that caring for the weak matters more than benefiting yourself.
exp.10:16:
It says that things will go very badly for the worthless shepherd, the one who abandons his sheep. A sword will fall on his arm and on his right eye. The arm stands for the strength to care for and defend, and the eye for the sight to guide and watch over. Both will become useless: the arm will wither (it will be paralyzed) and the eye will be darkened (it will be blind).

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. In this chapter God describes leaders who mistreat the people, and the verse before this one speaks of a shepherd who does not care for the weak sheep but takes advantage of them. Interpreters differ on which leader or leaders are meant; it is not certain to identify him with any particular named person.

For today: if you lead others, in the family, the church, or at work, remember that leading means caring, not taking advantage. Ask yourself who needs your attention and your help today.
exp.11:0:
This verse begins an important message from God about Israel. "Burden" here means a serious, weighty message, one that brings a warning or a sentence. Then God is presented as the one who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him. In other words, the one speaking is the Creator of everything, including the innermost part of each person.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile. Before announcing what is coming, which speaks of nations that will attack Jerusalem, God reminds the people who He is. Scholars interpret in various ways when and how that prophecy is fulfilled.

For today: when you face situations that seem bigger than you, remember that the God who made the heavens and formed you within still has control. You can entrust your fears to Him with peace.
exp.11:2:
It says that, on a future day, God will make Jerusalem a heavy stone for all the nations. Whoever tries to lift or carry it will be badly hurt and will be broken to pieces, that is, wounded and shattered. Even if all the peoples of the earth gather together against the city, they will not manage to overcome it. The city is called "Jerusalem" in its older spelling.

The Lord speaks, the Creator of the heavens, the earth, and the human spirit. He says this to a people who have gone through defeats and feel weak. Scholars understand "that day" in different ways: some see it as a future event, and others as an image of God's protection over his people. The central point is that God cares for his own.

For today: when you feel small before an enormous pressure, remember that your security does not depend on your strength, but on the God who sustains his people. Rest in him and pray with confidence.
exp.11:4:
It says that the leaders of Judah will realize in their hearts that their strength lies in the people of Jerusalem, but a strength that comes from the Lord of hosts, who is their God.

The leaders are the rulers, and the inhabitants are the people who live in the city.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He describes a future time when the nations will attack Jerusalem and God will protect it. Interpreters disagree about whether this is fulfilled in history, at the end of time, or in both senses. The central point is that the leaders recognize that victory comes from God, not from themselves.

For today: those who lead, at home, in the church, or at work, do well to lean on God and to value the people they serve. True strength is not one's own pride but trust in God together with mutual support.
exp.11:7:
In that day, the verse says, God himself will protect the people living in Jerusalem. Even the weakest among them will be strong like David, the warrior king. And the house of David will be like the angel of the Lord who goes before them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah after the exile, to a small people threatened by neighboring nations. "That day" refers to a future time when God intervenes. Interpreters understand it in different ways: as a promise for Israel, or as having a spiritual fulfillment. The following verse speaks of a spirit of grace and prayer.

For today: when you feel weak, remember that your strength does not depend on yourself but on God who sustains you. Pray with confidence and ask him for his help.
exp.11:9:
He says that God himself will pour out upon the people of Jerusalem, beginning with the family of King David, a spirit of grace, that is, of favor and compassion, and of prayer. Then they will look to God, the one they have pierced (wounded or run through), and they will mourn for him with a very deep sorrow, like someone who loses an only son or a firstborn son.

The LORD speaks in the middle of a promise of protection for Jerusalem against its enemies. After defending it, He brings something deeper: repentance. The passage is difficult, and the shift between "me" and "him" is understood in several ways. The New Testament (John 19:37) applies these words to Jesus on the cross.

For today: true repentance is a gift from God. Ask Him to give you a tender heart, to pray with sincerity, and to look to Christ with gratitude and humility.
exp.11:10:
It says there will be a great and deep mourning in Jerusalem, as intense as the mourning for Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon. "Jerusalem" here refers to Jerusalem. It is not known with certainty what Hadadrimmon refers to: some think of a place, others of a pagan god, and others connect it with the mourning for King Josiah, who died near Megiddon.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He announces that God will protect Jerusalem and will pour out the spirit of grace and of prayer on his people. Then they will look on the one they pierced and will mourn with repentance. Many Christians see Jesus here, and the New Testament quotes this passage in John 19:37.

For today: when we see our sin and look to Christ, we should not harden our hearts. We can mourn sincerely, ask for forgiveness, and receive the grace that God offers.
exp.12:1:
In that day, God says, he himself will remove idols from the land, so that not even their names are remembered anymore. He will also remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit, that is, an impure spiritual influence that pulls people away from God.

Speaking here is the LORD of hosts, the Lord with all power. This comes right after the promise of an open fountain that cleanses the sin of Jerusalem and of the house of David. Many Christians see in this a sign of Christ's work, although people disagree about how and when all of this is fulfilled. First God cleanses the heart, and then he removes what deceives.

For today: ask God to show you what has taken the place that belongs to him alone, and give it over to him with confidence.
exp.12:3:
It says that when that time comes, the false prophets will be ashamed of what they claimed to have seen from God. They will no longer put on the rough cloak, a garment of coarse hair like that worn by some true prophets, in order to deceive the people.

It is the LORD of hosts who speaks through Zechariah. On that day God promises to cleanse his people of idols and false prophecy. The verses that follow show a false prophet who denies being one and hides himself. Scholars debate the exact moment this refers to, but the central message is clear: God removes religious lies.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by the appearance of someone who speaks in God's name. Compare what you hear with the Bible and ask for wisdom to discern.
exp.13:0:
It says the day of the Lord is coming, that is, a time when God acts decisively. Here Jerusalem is told that its spoil, meaning what is taken from it after it has been defeated, will be divided in the midst of it, as if the enemies were sharing out the plunder before its eyes.

It is a prophecy from the book of Zechariah, in its final part. It speaks to Jerusalem, and the verses that follow describe a great battle and much suffering, but also that the Lord will go out to fight. Interpreters differ: some see it as something still future, others as symbolic language about God's judgment and deliverance.

For today: even when times are hard, we can trust that God has the last word. Rather than despair, we can pray and wait on Him with patience and hope.
exp.13:2:
After a time of great suffering for Jerusalem, the Lord himself will intervene. The reference to his going out is like a warrior heading into combat, and the word for the nations refers to the peoples of the earth. The phrase about fighting as he did in the day of battle recalls the times when God defended his people, although scholars debate which specific battle is meant.

The prophet Zechariah announces what will happen on the day of the Lord. First the nations attack Jerusalem, and then God acts. Many Christians see this as a prophecy about the end of time; others interpret it in a more symbolic way. All agree that the final word belongs to God, not to the enemies.

For today: when you feel that evil or hardships surround you, remember that God has not abandoned you. Trust that he is faithful, and while you wait, keep praying and doing good.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that, on a future day, the Lord will set his feet on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem. Then the mountain will split in two, from east to west, and a very great valley will form. One half will move toward the north and the other toward the south.

The prophet Zechariah speaks on God's behalf. Just before this, he describes an attack by the nations against Jerusalem, and then the Lord goes out to fight for his people. Christians interpret this in different ways: some see it as something literal that will happen at the return of Christ, and others see it as symbolic language of God's victory.

For today: even when the world seems to be in chaos, God still has the final word. You can rest in the assurance that he cares for his people and will keep his promises.
exp.13:6:
It says there will be a very special day, and that only God knows when it will come. It will not be like an ordinary day: there will be no clear light and no total darkness, and it will be neither exactly day nor night. But when it seems the day is about to end, at evening time, there will be light.

The prophet Zechariah is speaking, and this chapter announces the day when God will act, come to rescue his people, and reign over the whole earth. Interpreters differ on whether this refers to something in the future, to the time of Christ, or to both. What everyone recognizes is the message of hope in the middle of distress.

Today, when your situation seems confusing, neither clear nor dark, remember that God knows the times and can bring light right where you expected night. Trust him and keep waiting.
exp.13:7:
It says that, on the final day the prophet speaks of, living waters will flow out from Jerusalem. That means fresh, running water, not stagnant water. They will flow toward the east and toward the west. The eastern sea is usually understood to be the Dead Sea, and the western sea the Mediterranean. And they will flow all year round, in summer and in winter, never drying up.

The prophet Zechariah speaks here, announcing what God will do when He comes to reign. The chapter describes an extraordinary day, and the next verse says that the LORD will be king over all the earth. Many see in this an image of blessing and life flowing out from the presence of God. Interpreters differ on whether it will be fulfilled literally or symbolically.

For today: God is a source of life that never runs out. When you feel dry or weary, return to Him in prayer and trust, and let His life flow through you to others as well.
exp.13:9:
It says that the whole region around Jerusalem will become like a plain, from Geba (to the north) to Rimmon (to the south). Jerusalem, by contrast, will be raised up and will be inhabited in its place. Several gates and towers are named: Benjamin's Gate, the First Gate, the Corner Gate, the Tower of Hananel, and the king's winepresses.

The prophet Zechariah announces what God will do on that day, when the LORD reigns over all the earth. The place names mark the boundaries of the city. Some understand this literally, and others as an image of the security and honor of God's city.

For today: God promises to restore and care for what belongs to Him. Even if everything seems unstable to you right now, you can trust that He keeps His promises, and live with hope and peace.
exp.13:10:
It says that people will live in Jerusalem and that it will never again be under a curse. "Utter destruction" means something set apart for destruction or condemned by God. The city will be inhabited safely, that is, with security and without fear.

The prophet Zechariah speaks, in a vision of the day of the Lord, when God will reign over the whole earth. Before and after, there is talk of battles against Jerusalem and of judgment on its enemies. Some believers understand this as a promise for the future, others in a more symbolic way, but all see here God's final victory over evil.

For today: when you feel fear or insecurity, remember that God has the last word. Trust that He keeps His promises and rest in His care.
exp.13:11:
This verse describes a terrible punishment that God sends upon the nations that attacked Jerusalem. Their bodies waste away while they are still standing: the flesh rots, the eyes are consumed, and the tongue dissolves.

The prophet Zechariah announces what will happen on that day, when God intervenes at the end of time. Jerusalem will be protected and will dwell in safety. Interpreters differ on whether these images are literal or symbolic, but all agree that they show the power of God against those who oppose his people.

Today we can rest in the knowledge that God is just and cares for his own. We do not need to take revenge or live in fear, because he has the last word. Entrust your grievances to God in prayer, and let him bring about justice in his own way and in his own time.
exp.13:13:
This verse says that the people of Judah will also fight at Jerusalem, and that the wealth of the nations around them will be gathered together: gold, silver, and clothing, in great abundance. Clothing of this kind was valuable, a form of wealth in those days.

The prophet Zechariah describes the day of the LORD, when the nations attack Jerusalem and God intervenes in judgment. God is the one who gives the victory; Judah takes part, but does not win on its own. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future fulfillment, others as symbolic language of God's final triumph. The text does not clarify every detail.

For today: when you face a struggle, do your part with courage, but trust that the outcome is in God's hands. He can turn what seemed like loss into blessing, and everything ends in worshiping him.
exp.13:14:
This verse says that the same plague that falls on the enemy soldiers will also fall on their animals: horses, mules, camels, donkeys, and all the beasts in their camps. A plague is a blow or punishment sent by God. The pack and war animals were part of an army's military strength.

The prophet Zechariah speaks of that day, when the nations attack Jerusalem and God intervenes. The verses before describe confusion and panic among the enemies. Interpreters disagree: some see this as something still in the future, others as symbolic language about God's final victory.

For today: no human strength, resources, or strategy can compare with God. We can rest in the fact that He cares for His people and has the last word. Trust in Him before your own means.
exp.13:15:
The verse says that the survivors of the nations that attacked Jerusalem will not remain as enemies. Instead, every year they will go up to the city to worship God, whom it calls the King, the Lord of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles. That feast was a Jewish celebration of thanksgiving for the harvest and a remembrance of God's care in the wilderness.

Zechariah is a prophet who announces a future day of the Lord. After a great battle against Jerusalem, God himself intervenes and reigns over the whole earth. Christians interpret this passage in different ways: some see it as a literal scene of the future, others as a symbolic picture of Christ's reign.

Today we can learn that God can transform former adversaries into worshipers. Pray for someone who seems far from God, and worship the King with gratitude at all times, not only when everything is going well.
exp.13:16:
This verse says that the families of the earth who do not go up to Jerusalem to worship God, whom it calls King and Lord of hosts, will receive no rain. The word "go up" means to travel up to the city, and "worship" means to honor God with reverence. Rain was vital for the harvests.

The prophet Zechariah announces a future day when God will reign over the whole earth. The nations that once attacked Jerusalem will now go up each year to the Feast of Tabernacles, which recalled God's care and the harvest. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some literally, others as a picture of the universal worship of God.

Today we can remember that everything we receive, even the rain and the bread, comes from God. Ask yourself whether you truly honor him as King of your life. Thank him every day and seek to worship him with your community.
exp.11:12:
It says that on that day of great mourning, each family will mourn on its own: the clan of the house of Levi (the priests and temple servants) and the clan of Shimei, along with their wives. "Clan" means a family or lineage, and "on its own" means each group mourns separately.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. Earlier, in 12:10, he promises to pour out a spirit of grace and prayer, so that they will look to the one they pierced and mourn. Families of kings (David, Nathan) and of priests (Levi, Shimei) are named to show that no one is left out. It is not known with certainty which Shimei is meant, and it is interpreted in different ways. Many Christians see a reference to Christ here.

For today: true repentance is personal. No one repents for us, not even our family or church. Today you can set aside a moment alone to speak with God honestly.
exp.10:10:
It says that the agreement the shepherd had made was canceled on that very day, when he broke his staff called Favor. The afflicted of the flock, the humble people who were watching him closely, recognized that this act was the word of the LORD.

The prophet Zechariah speaks here, representing a shepherd appointed by God to care for a people who reject him. By breaking the staff, he shows that God withdraws his protection because of that hardness. Many Christians see here an anticipation of the rejection of Christ, and the New Testament connects the thirty pieces of silver with Matthew 27. Even so, interpreters debate the details.

For today: the humble who pay attention to God recognize his voice even in difficult moments. Cultivate a heart that is attentive and willing to listen, without hardening yourself when God corrects you.
exp.9:11:
God himself promises to give strength to his people. "I will strengthen them" means he will make them firm and powerful. "In the LORD" shows that this strength comes from being united with him. "In his name they will walk" means they will live in line with who God is, under his authority and representing him. And "declares the LORD" confirms that this is his promise.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. Earlier he had promised to gather his scattered people, who were in places such as Egypt and Assyria, and bring them back. He also announced the fall of the powers that oppressed them. Some understand this as a message about the return from exile, and others also see a future fulfillment. This verse closes the chapter with hope: God restores and sustains.

For today: do not depend only on your own strength. Before facing a challenge, ask God to strengthen you, and then take the steps of your day in a way that honors his name.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that the two olive branches, which supply oil through golden pipes, represent two "anointed ones," that is, two people set apart to serve God, who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.

The angel who was speaking with Zechariah answers his question about the vision of the golden lampstand and the two olive trees. Many believe it refers to Zerubbabel, the governor, and Joshua, the high priest, who led the rebuilding of the temple after the exile. Others see a broader or future reference. The text does not name them clearly here.

For today: God sustains his work with his Spirit, not only with human strength. We can serve him with humility, trusting that he supplies the oil, that is, the strength and guidance we need.
exp.7:1:
God says that he loves Zion with a very intense love. The word "jealous" means to care for what one loves with passion and not to tolerate that someone else takes it away. His "great fervor" shows his strong feeling against whatever was harming his people. It is a powerful zeal, born of love.

The Lord of Hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the exile in Babylon. The people had returned to Jerusalem, but they were discouraged and the city still lay in ruins. God reminds them that he has not forgotten them. His care is firm, and for that reason he promises to dwell among them again. Some understand his fervor as directed against the oppressing nations; others, as God's grief over the sin of his people.
