For today: when you feel far from God or discouraged, remember that he loves you with a passionate love and does not give up on you. Respond by drawing near to him with confidence and faithfulness.
exp.4:10:
The angel answers Zechariah's question: the two women carry the basket to the land of Shinar, which is Babylon. There a house will be built for it, and when it is ready, the basket will be set there on its pedestal. "Set" here means placed firmly in position.

The speaker is the angel who was accompanying the prophet in this vision. Inside the basket was a woman called "wickedness" (v. 8), a symbol of sin. Her removal to Babylon, a place associated in the Bible with rebellion and false worship, shows that God takes sin out from the midst of his people. Interpreters explain the details in different ways, but the general idea is clear.

For today: it is not enough to hide sin; we must ask God to remove it from our lives. Today you can confess something that is weighing on you and let him set it apart from you.
exp.11:11:
The verse says that the whole land will mourn, and it will do so in an orderly way: each clan on its own, with the clan of the house of David and their wives apart, and the clan of the house of Nathan and their wives apart. The family of King David is named, along with the family of Nathan, a son of David. A "clan" is a group of closely related families, and "will mourn" means that they will grieve with real pain.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He has just promised that he will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer, and that the people will look to the one they pierced. That weeping is one of repentance. It is compared to a well-known mourning, although scholars debate which one is meant. The New Testament connects this prophecy with Jesus (John 19:37).

For today: true repentance is personal. No one can weep on our behalf. Take a moment alone with God, without comparing yourself to others, and honestly lay before him what is in your heart.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that God will change how He treats the "remnant of this people," that is, the Jews who had returned from exile. In the past they lived through hard times, but now God will not treat them the way He did before. "The LORD of Hosts" is a title that presents the Lord as the ruler of all power, and "remnant" refers to the survivors who came back to their land.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, but they felt tired and afraid. Before the foundations were laid there had been scarcity, a lack of peace, and conflict. God encourages them to keep working and promises them blessing, peace, and the fruits of the land.

For today: if you are going through a difficult season, do not think it will always be this way. God can bring in a new time. In the meantime, keep faithfully and steadily doing what He has placed in your hands.
exp.7:19:
This verse announces that God will bring people from other nations and from many cities. "Peoples will yet come" means that this will happen in the future. The residents of those cities are the people who live in them. It is the beginning of a promise that continues in the following verses: those people will come to seek God.

The LORD of Hosts speaks, through the prophet Zechariah, to a people who had returned from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding. Earlier, God had promised them that their days of fasting and sorrow would turn into joy. Now he expands the promise: his blessing will draw others to him. Christians often see here a sign that God invites all nations.

For today: God wants others to seek him. Live with truth, peace and joy, and simply invite someone to know him.
exp.5:12:
He says that the Branch, a man whom God has promised, will build the temple of the Lord. He will be clothed in splendor, will sit down to rule on his throne, and will also be a priest on his throne. The verse says there will be peaceful counsel between the two roles, king and priest, which are described as working together in harmony.

God speaks through Zechariah after the return of the Jews from exile. Zechariah was to crown the priest Joshua as a symbolic sign. The title "Branch" is understood by many Christians as a sign pointing to Jesus, who is both king and priest. Some scholars think the message also looked toward Zerubbabel, the governor of that time. There are various interpretations.

Today we can trust that Jesus reigns and also represents us before God. If He leads your life with peace, you can rest, obey Him, and serve with hope in what God is building.
exp.10:13:
The passage says the prophet took his second staff, called "Union," and broke it. With that act he showed that the union between Judah and Israel, that is, between the two groups of God's people, was being broken. A staff is the shepherd's rod, and "brotherhood" means unity between brothers.

Zechariah speaks here as a shepherd who represents God. Earlier he had broken the staff "Grace" because the people rejected his care. Now the people value him at thirty pieces of silver, an insulting price. Breaking this second staff announces division as the consequence of that rejection. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of Jesus and the thirty coins of Judas (Matthew 27:9-10), although scholars debate the details.

For today: unity between brothers is precious and fragile. If there is division in your family or church, seek reconciliation, beginning with listening and asking forgiveness.
exp.11:6:
He says that the LORD will save the tents of Judah first, meaning the people of the countryside and the villages, who lived in simple houses, almost like campsites. He will do this so that the honor of David's family and of the people of Jerusalem is not greater than that of Judah. A dweller is someone who lives in a place.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah, in a promise about that day, when the nations attack Jerusalem. Scholars interpret that day in different ways: some see it in the history of Israel, others in the final time. God wants to prevent pride and keep his people united, so that some do not feel superior to others.

For today: God cares with special tenderness for those who seem less important. We can imitate him by valuing the humble, without boasting about what we have or achieve, and remembering that every victory comes from him.
exp.13:12:
On that final day of the battle against Jerusalem, God will send a great panic on the attacking peoples. It will be so intense that each soldier will seize the hand of another, and the hand of one will rise against the other. "A great panic from the LORD" means a fear or disorder that God sends; here "seize the hand" simply means to grab hold of someone.

Zechariah speaks on behalf of the Lord about a future day of the Lord, in which the nations attack Jerusalem and God defends her. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal event yet to come, others as symbolic language about God's final victory. In either case, the message to the people is comfort: God will not abandon them.

For today: when evil seems strong, we can trust that God has the last word. There is no need to repay evil with evil; we can rest in the knowledge that he does justice and cares for his own.
exp.1:10:
On that day, the verse says, many nations will join themselves to the Lord and become his people, not only Israel. God promises to live among his people in Jerusalem. "Will join themselves" describes nations that join, and "nations" refers to peoples who are not Jewish. "Will dwell among you" means God will live among them.

The prophet Zechariah speaks after the return from exile in Babylon. In the vision, a messenger sent by the Lord encourages Jerusalem to rejoice, because God himself will come to live with her. The phrase "has sent Me" is understood in several ways: some see the prophet, others see a divine messenger, and many Christians see a sign of Christ.

For today: God wants to dwell with his people, and his love reaches everyone. We can welcome people who are different from us with joy and remember that God is near. Today, pray for someone from another culture and greet them with affection.
exp.1:9:
God invites Jerusalem, called "Daughter of Zion," to shout for joy and be glad. The reason is a promise: the Lord himself is coming to live among his people. The phrase "I am coming to dwell among you" means God will be present with them.

Zechariah prophesies after the return from exile in Babylon. The people were few and discouraged while they rebuilt. The Lord speaks, and in the context the one who "sent me" appears to be a divine messenger. Many Christians see here a sign pointing to Christ, though this is an interpretation. The next verse promises that many nations will join themselves to God.

When you feel small or abandoned, remember that God promises to be near. Today you can set aside a few minutes to thank him and sing to him, not because everything is perfect, but because he is with you.
exp.0:13:
In this verse, the angel tells the prophet to proclaim a message from God: "I am very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion." The word "jealous" here means that God loves with intensity and defends what belongs to him. It is a passionate love, not an indifferent one.

Zechariah lives after the exile in Babylon, about seventy years of punishment. The angel had asked how much longer the sorrow and the ruin would last. God answers with words of comfort. He himself speaks through the angel and promises to return to his people, rebuild the temple, and protect the city.

For today: when you feel that God is far away or that your hard season will never end, remember that his love for his own is steady and passionate. You can bring him your question with honesty, as the angel did, and wait for his comfort.
exp.7:22:
This verse says that, in a future time, ten men from the nations of every tongue will tightly grasp the robe of a Jewish man. The phrase "tightly grasp the robe" means they will hold firmly onto his garment. They will say to him, "Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you."

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the people had returned from exile. God promises to restore Jerusalem and to draw many nations to seek him. The number ten probably expresses a large quantity, though this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: our lives can show God's presence in such a way that others feel a desire to know him. Live with humility, kindness and faith, and let your example raise questions about God.
exp.6:3:
Then the word of the LORD of Hosts came to Zechariah. This verse says that God answered with his word. It is a short phrase that opens God's answer.

Some men sent from Bethel asked whether they should keep weeping and fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for years. They were probably remembering the destruction of the temple. But God does not answer them directly. Instead, he speaks to Zechariah, and then asks whether those fasts were really for him.

For today: before practicing a religious custom, it is good to ask ourselves why we do it. God does not seek only rituals, but a sincere heart that honors him. We can pray: "Lord, teach me to do this for you."
exp.7:21:
This verse says that many peoples and mighty nations will come to Jerusalem to seek God, who is called here "the LORD of Hosts," meaning the LORD over all power. To "plead before the LORD" means to humbly ask for his mercy and help.

The prophet Zechariah speaks, passing on what God says. The people of Israel had just returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, with little strength and little hope. God promises them that Jerusalem will not be forgotten, and that other peoples will see that God is with them and will want to draw near to him.

For today: when others see us living with faith, humility, and hope, they may feel a desire to seek God. Let us live in such a way that our lives invite them to draw near to him.
exp.8:15:
On that day, the Lord their God will save his people as a shepherd saves his flock. They will be honored and lifted up in their land, sparkling like jewels in a crown. "Sparkling like jewels" means shining brightly, the way precious gems catch the light.

It is a prophecy from Zechariah, written after the return from exile. It speaks of God defending his people against their enemies and giving them peace and joy. Christians often see it fulfilled also in Christ, the good Shepherd, though it is interpreted in several ways. The following verse speaks of the goodness and beauty of God.

For today: if you feel small or unprotected, remember that God cares for you like a shepherd and gives you worth. Trust in his care and live with gratitude.
exp.12:4:
In that day, a man who was once known as a prophet will deny it. He will say that he is not a prophet but a farmer, and that he was bought and put to work as a servant when he was young.

The setting is a future day when God clears his people of false prophets and deceiving spirits. The disgrace is so great that even parents turn against the one who prophesied lies. The speaker here is the false prophet, who hides his past in order to save his life. The hairy cloak he once wore was a garment of hair, which some prophets used. Some interpreters see a reference to Christ in the verses that follow, but this is debated.

Today the verse invites us to be honest: not to use God's name to gain status or money. It is good to test what we hear against the Bible, and to speak of God with humility and truth.
exp.6:10:
This verse says the people refused to listen to God. The phrase "turned a stubborn shoulder" describes an ox that pulls back and will not let the yoke be put on it. The phrase "stopped up their ears" means they deliberately blocked their hearing so they would not take in what God said.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the Jews returned from exile. God reminds them what he had asked of their ancestors: true justice, mercy, and care for the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor. They did not obey, and so the punishment came. It is a warning so that they do not repeat the mistake.

For today: listening to God is not just hearing, but being willing to obey. Ask yourself whether there is something God is showing you, such as treating someone in need with kindness, that you are avoiding. Today you can open your heart and take one concrete step of mercy.
exp.9:8:
He says that God will scatter his people among the nations, like someone sowing seed. Even while they are far away, they will remember him. They will live with their children and come back to their land. The word translated "return" in this passage means "come back," and "sow" here speaks of scattering, with the idea that this seed will bear fruit.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He promises to restore Israel, here called Ephraim, the largest tribe of the northern kingdom. The people had suffered under bad shepherds and through being scattered. God says that he has redeemed them and will gather them again, from Egypt and Assyria. Scholars understand in various ways when this is fulfilled.

For today: even when you feel far away or scattered by your circumstances, God has not forgotten you. Remember him every day, and teach your children to remember him too.
exp.7:17:
This verse is a short introduction. It says that a message from God came to Zechariah, and God is called "the LORD of Hosts," a title that shows his power over all things. The phrase "came to me" means "the word reached me." It marks the beginning of a new message.

Zechariah was a prophet after the people returned from Babylon. God had just asked them for truth, justice, and hearts without evil. Now he answers a question about the fasts the people kept to remember the pain of the exile. God promises that these fasts will become days of joy.

For today: before seeking great things from God, let us listen carefully to his word. God wants what we do outwardly, such as praying or fasting, to go hand in hand with living in truth and peace with others.
exp.5:9:
God tells the prophet Zechariah to take an offering from three men who had come back from exile in Babylon: Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah. The same day, he is to go to the house of Josiah, son of Zephaniah. The "exiles" are the group of Jews who returned from Babylon.

The Lord speaks through Zechariah after the vision of the chariots. With the silver and gold these men brought, a crown was to be made for the high priest Joshua, as a prophetic sign of the Branch, the future Messiah. Christians often see Jesus there, as King and Priest. Some details about these men are not known with certainty.

Today we can learn that God uses the offerings and simple obedience of ordinary people to point to something great. Gladly place what you have, your time or your resources, at the service of God.
exp.0:10:
This verse reports what the riders sent by God had found. They say to the angel of the Lord, who was standing among the myrtle trees (shrubs with green, fragrant leaves), that they have patrolled the earth and all of it is at rest and tranquil, that is, at peace and without disturbance.

Zechariah has a vision at night. The riders are messengers who keep watch over the nations. Their report sounds peaceful, but God's people were still in ruins after the exile. That is why the angel immediately asks, "How long?" Many understand that this peace among the nations was not good news for Judah, which was hoping for restoration.

For today: the calm of the world does not always mean that everything is well. When you see injustice or a long wait, you can pray honestly, as the angel did, and trust that God answers with words of comfort.
exp.10:8:
Here the shepherd says he will stop caring for the flock. "I will no longer shepherd you" means "I am no longer going to look after you." Let the dying die, and let the perishing perish; and let those who remain devour one another's flesh. It is a picture of abandonment and total ruin.

The one speaking is the shepherd whom God placed in charge of his people. He grew weary of being rejected, and for that reason he withdraws his protection. Scholars debate who the "three shepherds" are and whom this shepherd represents. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ rejected, but this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when God's guidance is rejected, the community is destroyed by quarreling and selfishness. Value God's care, listen to his voice, and treat others with tenderness, not with bites.
exp.10:9:
He says the prophet took his shepherd's staff, called "Favor," and cut it in two. By this act he showed that he was revoking the covenant God had made with "all the nations." A "staff" is the shepherd's walking stick, and "cut it in two" is what the verse says in the first person.

Zechariah acts as a shepherd on God's behalf, and the people reject his care. Breaking the staff stands for God withdrawing his protection because the people despised him. That is why, right afterward, they pay him thirty pieces of silver. Christian interpreters see here a sign that points to Jesus and his betrayal; others read it mainly within the history of Israel. Who the "three shepherds" are is not known for certain.

For today: let us not take God's care for granted. Let us value his guidance with gratitude and obedience, and listen to his voice as he speaks to us.
exp.7:6:
He says that God himself will rescue his people. He speaks of "the land of the east" and "the land of the west." It is a way of saying that he will bring them back from every place where they are scattered. Here "save" means "I will save" or "I will rescue."

The LORD of Hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people had returned from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding the temple, but they felt weak and discouraged. God promises that Jerusalem will once again have peace, with children playing in its streets.

For today: when what God has promised seems too difficult, remember that nothing is too hard for him. Trust in his faithfulness, pray with hope, and keep doing with courage what he has placed in your hands, even if you do not yet see the full result.
exp.9:3:
From Judah, the people God will visit, will come the leaders and the strength they need. The "cornerstone" is the firm leader who holds everything together. The "tent peg" is the peg that secures the tent, a picture of stability. The "battle bow" speaks of strength for fighting, and the "ruler" is the one who governs and makes demands. Many see here a promise of the Messiah; others see a promise of good leaders in general.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people had been deceived by idols, diviners and bad shepherds, and wandered like sheep without a guide. God promises to care for his flock and to give them leaders and strength from within his own house, not from foreign help.

For today: when you feel adrift or without strength, do not look for security in empty voices or in what promises much. Turn to God, who is faithful to sustain you and to raise up what you need.
exp.6:7:
This verse is a short phrase that introduces a message. It says that the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah. The word "came" is related to the verb "was" in the text, and "word of the LORD" means a message that God himself gave him.

Here the speaker is God, who speaks through Zechariah. The people had asked whether they should continue their religious fasts. In the verses before this one, God reminds them that what matters is not only the ritual but the heart. This verse prepares the message that follows: to practice justice and mercy and to care for the most vulnerable.

For today: before we worry about our religious practices, let us ask how we treat the people around us. Today you can help someone who needs it, such as a neighbor, a family member, or a foreigner, and in this way put into practice what God asks.
exp.5:14:
It says that people from far-off places will come and help build the temple of the LORD. When that happens, the people will know that the LORD of Hosts has sent the prophet to them. The promise will come true if they diligently obey the voice of the LORD their God.

Zechariah speaks to the people who returned from exile in Babylon, when rebuilding the temple was difficult. Shortly before, the prophet speaks of the Branch who will build the temple and will be both king and priest. Many Christians see in this a sign pointing to Jesus; others emphasize first Joshua and Zerubbabel. The "far away" may be Jews scattered abroad, or also other nations.

For today: God continues to build his work with people from every place, but he calls us to obedience. This week, listen to his Word and practice one concrete step of obedience, even if it seems small.
exp.13:8:
The verse says that the LORD will be recognized and obeyed as King over the whole earth. "The LORD alone, and His name alone" means that there will no longer be rivals to his rule or confusion about who the true God is. Everyone will know him for who he is.

Zechariah, a prophet after the return from exile, announces a future "day of the LORD." Earlier he spoke of battles against Jerusalem; now he shows God's final victory, with living waters flowing out of the city and lasting peace. Christians often see this fulfilled in the final reign of Christ; others interpret it in different ways, and not everyone agrees on the details.

For today: if one day the whole earth will recognize God as King, today I can put him first in my life, without dividing my heart among many "gods" such as money, pride, or fear.
exp.7:18:
This verse says that the fasts the people kept each year, in the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months, will become times of joy, gladness and cheerful feasts. The phrase "will become" means these days will be turned into something new. At the end, God tells his people: "Therefore you are to love both truth and peace."

The Lord of Hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile in Babylon. Many understand that these fasts remembered the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple, though the details of each date are explained in several ways. God promises to restore his people, but he also asks them to live with a sincere and just life.

For today: God can turn our times of pain into joy, but he wants us to live with honesty and peace. Today you can choose to speak the truth and seek reconciliation with someone close to you.
exp.7:9:
The verse describes what life was like before the people set about rebuilding the temple. The phrase "neither man nor beast received wages" means that work brought no reward, whether for people or for animals. "Nor was there safety from the enemy for anyone who came or went" refers to anyone who moved about: there was no security. On top of that, there were enemies, and the people were also turned against one another.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah to the Jews who had returned from exile. The work on the temple had stopped for a time, and the people were living in scarcity and fear. God reminds them of their difficult past to encourage them to keep going, because he promises that what is coming will be different: peace and fruit from the land.

For today: when your effort seems to bear no fruit, remember that God can change the seasons. Put first what matters to him, work with steadiness, and seek peace with those around you.
exp.0:2:
He says that God invites his people to return to him. "Return to me" means to leave the wrong path and seek him again. And God promises, "I will return to you," meaning he too will draw near. The words "the LORD of Hosts" show that the one calling has all power.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, around the year 520 BC. The people had come back from exile in Babylon, and their ancestors had suffered for disobeying. God does not want that story repeated, so he offers a fresh start before the temple is rebuilt.

For today: if you feel you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you have sorted yourself out first. Take one simple step today, such as praying honestly, and trust that he responds with grace.
exp.12:0:
This verse announces that a time will come when God will open a fountain, like a spring that is always flowing, for the royal family of David and for all the people of Jerusalem. That fountain is there to cleanse them from sin and impurity, the things that separate us from God.

The prophet Zechariah speaks, passing on what the LORD says. It comes after announcements about the people's repentance (chapter 12). Many Christians see here a sign of the forgiveness offered through Jesus; others connect it with a future restoration of Israel. The following verses show that this cleansing includes giving up idols and false prophecies.

For today: you do not have to make yourself presentable before approaching God. Come with your guilt and your stains, trusting that his forgiveness is open and available, and also let go of whatever pulls you away from him.
exp.12:6:
It says that God himself calls on the sword to strike his Shepherd, whom he calls "the man who is my Companion," meaning someone very close to him. When the Shepherd is struck, the sheep will be scattered. The sheep being scattered means they will be spread apart. The little ones are the small, the weak of the flock, on whom God turns his hand, either to care for them or to purify them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The preceding context deals with false prophets and with wounds received in the house of friends. Scholars debate who this Shepherd is. Jesus quoted this verse before his arrest (Matthew 26:31), and many Christians see it fulfilled in him. What follows shows a people tested like gold in the fire.

For today: When everything is shaken and you feel scattered, remember that God does not let go of the little ones; trust that he tests you to draw you closer to himself.
exp.3:4:
The angel asks Zechariah whether he understands what he has just seen: a golden lampstand with two olive trees beside it. Zechariah answers honestly: "No, my lord." The word "lord" is a respectful way of addressing the angel.

Zechariah was a prophet after the return from exile in Babylon. The people were rebuilding the temple and felt weak and discouraged. God gives him a vision, and the angel explains that the work, led by Zerubbabel, would not be accomplished by human strength but by the Spirit of God. Many understand the oil as a symbol of the Spirit, though the details of the olive trees are interpreted in various ways.

For today: do not be afraid to say "I do not understand" before God. Ask with humility, and he will teach you. Also, trust that his Spirit can sustain what you cannot accomplish alone.
exp.4:4:
The angel who had been explaining the visions to Zechariah came forward again and told him, "Now lift up your eyes and see what is approaching." It is an invitation to look carefully at a new vision.

Zechariah is a prophet who speaks to the people who returned from exile. God gives him visions, and an angel explains them. Just before this, he saw a flying scroll, which showed that God judges theft and false oaths. Now another vision begins. Its exact meaning is understood in several ways, so it is good to read it with humility.

For today: God invites us to look with attentive and sincere eyes. Ask him to show you what in your life is not honest, such as a small lie or a broken promise, and leave it in his hands to change.
exp.11:13:
It says that, on that day of mourning, all the remaining clans will also weep, each clan on its own, and the wives of each clan separately. A "clan" here means a household or extended family group. "Separately" means each group on its own.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. In the verses before, he announces that he will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer, and that the people will look on the one they pierced and mourn for him (12:10). The names of David, Nathan, Levi and Shimei represent royal and priestly families. Christian interpreters often connect this passage with Christ, although some see it in relation to the history of Israel.

For today: true repentance is personal. It is not enough to weep as a group or simply follow the crowd. Take some time alone with God, and also within your family, to acknowledge your failings and seek his forgiveness.
exp.4:2:
It says the flying scroll represents a curse, meaning a judgment from God, that is going out over the whole land. One side of the scroll names the punishment for the thief, and the other side names the punishment for the person who swears falsely. The phrase "face of the whole earth" refers to the surface of the land.

The one speaking is the angel who accompanies Zechariah during his visions. God himself later explains that he will send that curse into the house of the thief and of the one who swears falsely in his name. Both sins break God's law: one harms one's neighbor, and the other misuses God's name. Some think the size of the scroll, about 9 by 4.5 meters, recalls the holy place of the temple, but that is an interpretation.

Today, God invites us to live with honesty: not to take what belongs to others and to keep our word. Think of a promise you made and keep it.
exp.2:7:
God calls Joshua the high priest, along with his companions seated before him, to listen closely. He says they are a sign, showing that something greater is coming. God then promises to bring his servant, the Branch, a term for a shoot growing up from a root.

These words come from the angel of the LORD, spoken after Joshua has been cleansed of his filthy clothing and restored to his place. This happens while the people are returning from exile and rebuilding the temple. Many Christians see in the Branch a promise of the Messiah, Jesus, and the verses that follow speak of removing sin in a single day.

For today: God does not leave us in our past or in our failures, but points us to Christ. Today you can trust that his forgiveness is real, and live with peace and grateful obedience.
exp.12:8:
God says that a third of the people will pass through the fire, the way silver and gold are heated to burn away what is impure. The phrase "I will test them" means "I will put them to the test." After that, these people will call on God's name, he will answer them, and he will say, "They are my people." They will respond, "The Lord is our God."

The one speaking is the LORD of hosts, through the prophet Zechariah. The passage just before this one speaks of a struck shepherd and scattered sheep, and many Christians connect it with Jesus (Matthew 26:31). Others understand it as a reference to the history of Israel. What is clear is that God refines a faithful remnant to restore their relationship with him.

For today: when you go through a trial, do not think that God has abandoned you. You can call on him with confidence, believing that he hears you and that, even in pain, he still claims you as his own.
exp.5:8:
It says that God spoke again to the prophet Zechariah. The phrase "the word of the LORD also came to me" means "a message from the LORD came to me." It is a simple phrase, but it marks the beginning of a new instruction from God.

Zechariah is the one speaking, and he tells that he received this message after the vision of the chariots and the horses that went through the earth. That vision ended by showing that God's judgment reached Babylon, the north country. Now God gives a specific command: to take silver and gold from the Jews who returned from exile and make crowns for the priest Joshua. Many believe this points to the coming Messiah, though it is explained in different ways.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before acting, take a moment to read the Bible and listen carefully to what he tells you.
exp.8:14:
God promises to protect his people. "Shield" means that he will care for them and guard them. The people will overcome their enemies and destroy them with slingstones, so their weapons will not harm them (this phrase is understood in several ways). They will roar with joy, like people who have been drinking wine. They will be drenched like the corners of the altar, which were splashed with the blood of the sacrifice.

The prophet Zechariah speaks on God's behalf to a small people, surrounded by powerful nations. He mentions Greece as an enemy. Some see fulfillments of this in history, and others see a announcement of the time of the Messiah. Scholars do not fully agree.

Today we can remember that our security is not in our own strength, but in God. When you face something difficult, pray and trust in his care, and let gratitude fill you with joy.
exp.1:7:
God says that, after showing his glory, he will send his messenger against the nations that have plundered his people. He gives the reason: whoever touches Israel touches the apple of his eye, that is, the pupil, the most delicate and carefully guarded part of the eye. To plunder means to rob or pillage. The meaning of the phrase "after His glory" is understood in several ways, and its exact sense is not certain.

The Lord speaks through a messenger, probably in a vision given to Zechariah. The Jews were returning from exile in Babylon, and God promises them protection and nearness as they rebuild. Exactly who the messenger is also is interpreted in different ways.

For today: if you feel small or vulnerable, remember that God cares for you with tenderness. Rest in his protection and let him take care of justice, without returning evil for evil.
exp.3:6:
It says that a huge obstacle, compared to a "great mountain," will be leveled before Zerubbabel. He will bring out the capstone, the top stone, while the people shout, "Grace, grace to it!" That is, they ask for God's favor on the work. "Becoming a plain" means becoming level ground.

An angel speaks to Zechariah with a message from the LORD for Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah after the exile in Babylon. The people were rebuilding the temple amid opposition and weariness. The mountain represents those difficulties; the text does not say precisely what they refer to. Earlier, God said: "Not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit."

For today: when a good task from God seems impossible, do not rely on your own strength alone. Keep moving forward in faith, pray for his help, and thank him for every step forward as a gift of his grace.
exp.7:14:
God says that, just as he once decided to punish his people, he has now changed course and has resolved to do good to Jerusalem and Judah. The word "turning" means returning or changing direction, and "I have resolved" means I have made up my mind. And he tells them: "Do not be afraid."

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people had returned from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding the temple, amid discouragement and fear. God reminds them that their earlier punishment was real, but that now his purpose is to bless them. He then asks them to live with truth, justice, and without evil against their neighbor.

For today: if God is leading you into a new beginning, do not let fear of the past paralyze you. Trust in his goodness and respond with honesty and good treatment toward others.
exp.7:4:
This verse describes the streets of Jerusalem filled with boys and girls playing there. It is a simple scene of peace and joy.

The verse's wording is "boys and girls," and "the city" refers to Jerusalem.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile in Babylon. The city was weak and the people were discouraged. God promises to dwell in the middle of it. Together with the elders sitting in the squares, the children playing show a city that is secure, with life in every age. Interpreters see here a promise for that time and also a fuller hope for the future.

For today: God is concerned with the everyday and the simple. We can pray for the safety of the children in our community and make sure they have healthy places to grow up and play.
exp.10:15:
God says he will allow a bad shepherd to rise up over the people. This shepherd does not care for the sheep: he does not go after the lost ones, he does not seek the young, he does not heal the broken, nor does he sustain the healthy. Instead, he devours the flesh of the choice sheep and tears off their hooves, which shows that he uses them without limit.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He has just broken the staff called "Bonds", and the people are left without unity or good care. Many understand this as a warning against unjust leaders; others connect it to the rejection of the Good Shepherd. Interpreters do not agree on everything.

Today: if you lead or influence others, care for them as God cares, with patience and service, especially for the weak.
exp.9:4:
God's people will be like brave soldiers who trample their enemies as if they were mud in the street. They will win the battle because the Lord is with them. By contrast, the cavalry, who seemed the most powerful, will be put to shame.

Speaking through the prophet Zechariah, the Lord addresses a people who were discouraged and misled by bad shepherds, that is, leaders. God promises to care for Judah as his flock and restore its strength. Horses were a symbol of the military power of the nations. Some understand this as a promise for its own time, while others also see in it a hope for the future.

Today, when you feel weak before a great problem, remember that your strength does not depend on your resources, but on God being with you. Pray, and take the next step with confidence.
exp.11:8:
It says that on that day, God himself will set out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. "I will set out to destroy" means that God will determine to break the power of those nations that attack the city. "Nations" means the peoples or nations, and "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. In the verses before this one, he promises to protect Judah and Jerusalem and to strengthen even the weakest among them. Then the text goes on to speak of an outpouring of grace and repentance. Interpreters debate whether all of this refers to the final future or to nearer events; Christians often also see a reference to Christ in the words about the one they pierced.

For today: when you feel weak or surrounded by problems, remember that God cares for his people. Rest in his protection, pray with humility, and trust that he works in his own time.
exp.11:1:
He says God will make Jerusalem a cup of drunkenness to all the surrounding peoples. The image is of a drinking vessel that leaves people staggering. When the nations around Jerusalem come against it, they will be left reeling, like someone who has drunk too much and cannot keep their footing. Judah and Jerusalem will both be under siege.

The LORD is presented as the Creator of the heavens, the earth, and the human spirit. The message is a "burden," that is, a solemn message. It was given to a people who felt surrounded and weak. Scholars debate whether it refers to an event near the time of the prophet or to a time still in the future. What is certain is the message: God protects his people.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, remember that the God who sustains the universe also cares for his own. Pray with confidence and rest in Him.
exp.8:6:
This verse says that God himself will cleanse the Philistines of their detestable practices. The phrase about the blood refers to meat with the blood still in it, something forbidden to Israel, and "abominations" speaks of foods and customs tied to idol worship. God says he will remove the blood from their mouths and the abominations from between their teeth. Those who remain will belong to God and will become like a clan in Judah, and Ekron will be like the Jebusites, an ancient people of Jerusalem who were absorbed into Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah. Earlier he had announced judgment on the Philistine cities. Here the judgment turns into purification and hope. Interpreters explain the detail about the Jebusites in several ways, but all of them see a promise of inclusion. Shortly afterward appears the humble king who comes riding on a donkey.

For today: God not only corrects, he also cleanses and adopts. We can trust that no one is too far away to be received, and we should treat those we see as distant with that same hope.
exp.5:11:
God tells the prophet Zechariah to say to the high priest Joshua that a man is coming whose name is the Branch. This man will branch out from where he is and will build the temple of the LORD.

The one speaking is the LORD of Hosts, the LORD who has all power. The people had come back from exile in Babylon and were rebuilding the temple. Zechariah performs a symbolic crowning of Joshua, who represents someone greater than himself. Many Christians see Jesus, the Messiah, as both king and priest in this passage. Others think it also looked toward Zerubbabel, and this is debated.

For today: God carries out his plans even when what we see seems small or slow. Trust that he is still building his work, and offer him your hands to take part in it with patience.
exp.13:5:
That verse says that on "that day," the day when God acts in a special way, there will be no ordinary light. Some translations render it differently, and the wording here is hard to pin down, so there is room for different readings of what this means.

The prophet Zechariah speaks of "the day of the LORD," when God will come to Jerusalem with his holy ones, the Mount of Olives will split apart, and the people will flee. Scholars interpret this in different ways: some see a future event, others see symbolic language. What is clear is that God acts and the natural order is shaken. The next verse adds that at evening there will be light.

For today: there are confusing moments, without clear answers, when the light seems to be missing. Trust that God knows that day and can bring light "in the evening time." Rest in him while you wait.
exp.9:9:
God promises that he will bring back his scattered people. He will bring them back from Egypt and gather them from Assyria, two places where they had been enslaved or exiled. He will bring them to Gilead and Lebanon, regions east and north of Israel. The phrase "I will bring them back" means that he will return them, and "bring them" is his promise to lead them home. The words "until no more room is found for them" mean that the land will become too small for them, because the people will grow greatly.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the exile. He encourages a small and fragile people with the promise that God has redeemed them and does not forget them. Egypt and Assyria represent places of oppression. Some see here a fulfillment that is still in the future, and others see images of the restoration that God carries out with his people.

For today: if you feel far away or lost, remember that God knows how to gather and restore. Trust that his care is greater than your story, and return to him.
exp.11:5:
In that day, God says, he will make the clans of Judah like a firepot in a woodpile, like a flaming torch among the sheaves. They will consume all the peoples around them, on the right and on the left, while the people of Jerusalem remain secure there.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He announces a future time, "that day," when Jerusalem is attacked by many nations. The clans of Judah recognize that their strength comes from God. Some see this as fulfilled at the end of time, and others as a picture of God's protection in general.

For today: when you feel small before a great problem, remember that your strength is not in yourself or your resources, but in God. Trust in him, and also lean on your community of faith.
exp.10:12:
Here God tells the prophet to throw the thirty pieces of silver, the wage the people paid him, to the potter. God calls it a "magnificent price," but the words are ironic, because such a small sum is an insulting value to place on the worth of the Shepherd. The people valued him as a mere hireling. Zechariah obeys and throws the silver down in the house of the LORD.

The LORD speaks, and Zechariah acts as a shepherd who represents God before a people who reject him. His wage of thirty pieces shows how little value they gave to his care. The New Testament links this passage with Judas and the thirty coins (Matthew 27:3-10), and many Christians read it that way.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we value God with generosity or only with what is left over. Let us give him first place, with gratitude and sincerity.
exp.9:2:
My anger burns against the shepherds, that is, the leaders who were supposed to care for the people. God says he will also punish the leaders who go at the front of the flock. But the LORD of Hosts attends to His flock, the house of Judah, and will care for them himself. He will make them like His royal steed in battle, strong and fine.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people had turned to idols and fortune-tellers, who offered false comfort, and their leaders did not guide them well. Because of this, the people wandered like sheep without a shepherd. God responds by correcting those leaders and promising to care for his people.

For today: do not place your hope only in leaders or in empty comforts. Seek the LORD, the good Shepherd, and pray with confidence. He attends to his own and gives them strength.
exp.9:0:
Ask the LORD for rain in the springtime, and He will answer. This verse says the people should ask God for the spring rain that came before the harvest. God promises to make storm clouds, send showers of rain, and give crops in the field to everyone.

The prophet Zechariah speaks in God's name to a people who had returned from exile. The verses that follow show the problem: some were looking for answers in idols and diviners, who offer false comfort. That is why the people wandered like sheep without a shepherd. The prophet reminds them that rain comes from the LORD, not from images or lies.

For today: instead of rushing first to other sources of security, bring your specific needs to God in prayer. Ask Him with confidence, even when you are already expecting provision, and thank Him for what He has already given you.
exp.1:6:
God calls Zion, that is, his people, to get up and escape from Babylon. "Dwell" means "live," and "Get up" and "Escape" mean "get out and get to safety." The verse says "the Daughter of Babylon" because some Jews were still living there, among the Babylonians.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Zechariah. This was after the exile, while Jerusalem was being rebuilt. Many Jews were still far away. God promises them that he will be a wall of fire around his city and will care for them as the apple of his eye. That is why he invites them to return and not to remain in a place that was not their home.

Today, God invites us not to settle into surroundings or habits that pull us away from him. Ask him for courage to leave behind whatever holds you back, and trust that his care goes with you when you take the step.
exp.7:20:
This verse describes the people of one city going to another and urging one another: "Let us go at once to plead before the LORD and to seek the LORD of Hosts." Pleading before the LORD means humbly asking for his mercy and kindness. The one who invites adds, "I myself am going," showing that he does not only encourage others but goes along with them.

The LORD of Hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile. The fasts had recalled past tragedies, and God promises to turn them into feasts of joy. He then announces that many peoples will come to seek him. How and when this is fulfilled is understood in several different ways by interpreters.

For today: it is not enough to tell others to seek God; invite them and go with them. Today you can invite a relative or friend to pray or to gather with a congregation, and accompany them yourself.
exp.5:6:
The horses were strong, and they set out eager to go. The LORD gave the command: "Go and patrol the earth," and they went out and patrolled the earth.

Zechariah sees a vision of chariots and horses. The angel explains that they are the four winds or spirits of heaven, sent out by the Lord of all the earth. The text does not name clearly who gives the order; it is understood that he acts with God's authority. The verses that follow suggest that the north, from which Israel's enemies came, receives judgment.

Today: when the world seems out of control, remember that God rules over all the earth and nothing escapes him. Trust in him and obey with the same readiness as those horses.
exp.5:10:
God tells the prophet Zechariah to take silver and gold, make an ornate crown, and set it on the head of the high priest, Joshua son of Jehozadak. The high priest is the chief priest. The verse says "crown" in the singular, but some scholars believe it may describe a single crown made from several pieces.

The Lord speaks after a series of visions that Zechariah has received. The silver and gold come from Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. This takes place while the temple is being rebuilt. Joshua receives a crown, which is unusual for a priest, and so it points toward the "Branch," who will be both king and priest. Many Christians see Jesus in this.

For today: Jesus joins service to God with his authority. We can trust that he guides us with peace, and that our small contributions also matter in his work.
exp.6:6:
This verse is a question that God asks his people. It reminds them that he had already spoken before, through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem and its surrounding towns were populous and prosperous, and the Negev and the foothills were inhabited. "Proclaimed" means that he made his message known.

God speaks through Zechariah, after the return from exile. Some people were asking whether they should keep fasting because of the destruction of Jerusalem. God answers that what mattered was not the fasting, but obeying what he had already said. The verses that follow explain what he asked for: justice, mercy, and compassion.

For today: before asking whether we keep certain religious practices, let us examine how we treat people. This week, look for one concrete way to be just and compassionate toward someone close to you.
exp.9:1:
This verse says that the idols spoke deceit, and that the diviners saw illusions and told false dreams. Their comfort is empty and does no good. Because of this the people wandered like sheep, oppressed because they had no shepherd to guide them. Here "idols" are the household images, called teraphim, and "empty" means something without real substance or worth.

The prophet Zechariah speaks in the name of the LORD to the Jews who returned from exile. He has just told them to ask God for rain, not the idols. Then he contrasts the false guides with God, who will care for his flock. The "shepherds" are their leaders.

For today: before following any voice that promises comfort, such as horoscopes, spiritual fads, or seductive leaders, ask yourself whether it leads you to God. He is the one who truly cares for us.
exp.11:3:
God says that, "on that day," he will strike the war horses with panic and their riders with madness. "Panic" means sudden, overwhelming fear, and "madness" means losing one's grip on reason. By contrast, God promises to keep a watchful eye on Judah: he will watch over the house of Judah with care.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He promises protection to Jerusalem and Judah when many nations gather together against them. "That day" points to a future time, and interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it in the history of Israel, and others in the end of times. The horse represents the military power of that era.

For today: when you feel that the forces against you are greater than your own, remember that God keeps watch over you with care. Trust in him and not only in your own resources.
exp.1:5:
It says God urgently calls his people: "Get up! Get up! Flee from the land of the north!" The north is named here as the place they must leave. God reminds them that it was he who scattered them like the four winds of heaven, that is, in every direction. Now he invites them to come back out from there.

It is part of a vision given to the prophet Zechariah, after the exile in Babylon. The LORD speaks. Babylon lay to the north of Israel along the route of entry, and that is why it is called "the land of the north." Many Jews were still living there even though they could already return. God wants them to go back to Jerusalem, where he promises to protect them like a wall of fire.

For today: if God calls you to leave something that binds you or pulls you away from him, do not stay comfortable. Obey his call, because he himself will watch over you on the way.
exp.7:13:
God says that just as he decided to bring disaster on his people when their forefathers angered him with their disobedience, and he did not change his mind, so now he has also decided to do them good. "Provoked me to anger" means that they made him angry. "I did not relent" means that he did not back down from his decision.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah to the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon. They were discouraged and afraid while they rebuilt the temple. God reminds them that his earlier judgment was firm and real, and that is why his promise of blessing is also certain. He tells them: "Fear not."

For today: if God keeps what he says, we can trust his promises even when we feel weak or afraid. Today, hand God one specific fear and take a step of obedience, trusting that his word does not fail.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that in the future day of cleansing, if anyone still prophesies falsely, his own father and mother will reject him. They will say to him, "You shall not remain alive, because you have spoken falsely in the name of the LORD." The verse of the words "pierce him through" is that they describe a wound made with a spear. It is a very harsh scene.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. After promising a fountain of forgiveness and cleansing, he announces that he will remove the idols and the false prophets. The law of Moses commanded that the false prophet be punished (Deuteronomy 13 and 18). It is interpreted in several ways: some see it as zeal for the truth in Israel, and others relate it to the time of the Messiah. The language is strong on purpose.

For today: God's truth matters more than any family tie or custom. Examine what you hear in God's name and compare it with the Bible, with humility and without violence.
exp.1:12:
It says that all people must be silent and show reverence before God, because he has roused himself to act from his holy dwelling, which is heaven. The word translated "be silent" is rendered simply as "be silent" in your verse, and "all people" means all of humanity. The phrase about God roused into action is a vivid way of saying that God is moving to act.

This verse closes the vision in Zechariah 2. The prophet speaks after the return from exile in Babylon, when Jerusalem was still being rebuilt. God promises to dwell among his people, to draw many nations to himself, and to choose Jerusalem once again. That is why the call to silence is an act of reverence: God himself is about to intervene.

For today: before you worry about everything or offer your opinion on it all, take a few minutes of silence before God. Acknowledge that he is acting and still working, even if you cannot see it yet. Trust that he keeps his promises.
exp.13:18:
This verse says there will be a penalty for Egypt and for all the nations that do not go up to Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles. The word "penalty" means punishment, and the "nations" are the peoples or countries of the world. This feast remembered the time when Israel lived in temporary shelters in the wilderness and God provided for them. In the verses just before, the punishment described is a lack of rain.

Zechariah speaks of "that day," a future time when God will rule over all the earth. Egypt is named on its own, perhaps because it depended on the Nile river and not so much on rain, although interpreters explain this in different ways. There is also debate about whether this will be fulfilled literally or symbolically.

Today we can learn that worshiping God is not optional or something to put off for later. We depend on Him for everything, so let us give thanks to Him regularly and in obedience.
exp.13:1:
God says he himself will gather all the nations to fight against Jerusalem. The city will be captured, the houses looted, and the women violated. Half of the people will be taken away into exile, but the rest will not be removed from the city.

The prophet Zechariah speaks of "the day of the LORD," a time of judgment and of God's final victory. The verse that follows shows that God will then fight for his people. Interpreters differ: some see this as a future event still to come, and others as symbolic language or as already fulfilled in part.

Even in times of pain and chaos, God does not lose control or abandon his own. You can rest in the knowledge that, after the trial, he has the last word. Today, pray with confidence and remain faithful to him.
exp.1:3:
One angel tells another to run and tell "that young man," the one who was going to measure Jerusalem, that the city will be a place without walls. It will be filled with so many people and livestock that a wall could not contain them.

Zechariah sees this vision at night, after the exile in Babylon. A young man goes out with a measuring line to measure the city and plan its rebuilding. An angel stops him, because God has greater plans. Then God himself promises to be a wall of fire all around the city and its glory within it. Some understand the young man to be the prophet himself; others see him as an unnamed figure.

For today: let us not place our trust only in our defenses or plans. God cares for his people and can give them more than we imagine. Entrust your fears and your limits to him today.
exp.8:16:
He says that God's loveliness and beauty are immense, and that He shows them in abundance. The grain and the new wine are images of provision and joy. "Young men" are the young men, and "young women" are the young women. In this way, all the people, even the youngest, will enjoy what God gives.

Zechariah speaks on God's behalf to the people of Israel, after the exile. The verses before it promise protection, victory and restoration: God will care for his people like a flock. There are several ways to understand "how lovely they will be": some see it as God's loveliness, others as that of the restored people. Many Christians also see here a sign of the Messiah.

For today: when you receive your daily bread, pause and give thanks to God. His goodness is seen in simple things, and giving thanks helps you live with joy and trust.
exp.10:4:
It describes the people as a flock in the hands of those without compassion. The buyers would slaughter them without remorse. The sellers grew rich and even praised the Lord for it. The shepherds, who were supposed to care for them, showed them no compassion either. The phrase "without remorse" means that the buyers felt no sorrow or regret for what they did.

God speaks through the prophet Zechariah, who receives the command to tend the flock doomed to slaughter. The sheep represent the oppressed people, and the shepherds represent their leaders. Scholars debate exactly which group each one refers to, but the message is clear: God sees the injustice of the leaders and announces judgment.

For today: let us examine whether what we gain harms others. We must never use God's name to justify unjust gain. If we care for others, let us do it with compassion.
exp.3:12:
The angel asks Zechariah whether he does not understand what he has seen, and Zechariah answers honestly, "No, my lord." His reply shows respect toward the angel, and it is a plain admission of not knowing.

Zechariah is seeing a vision: a golden lampstand with olive trees that supply it with oil. An angel explains its meaning. The message of this chapter is that the work of rebuilding the temple would not advance by human strength, but "by my Spirit" (v. 6). The two "sons of oil" are usually understood to be Zerubbabel and Joshua, although some see them in another way.

For today: there is nothing wrong with admitting that we do not understand. Zechariah said "I do not know," and God taught him. We can approach the Bible with humility and ask God to explain it to us.
exp.4:0:
Zechariah says that he looked up and saw a flying scroll. In his vision he was shown a scroll in the air in front of him, which was a rolled-up written document, like the books of that time. It is the fourth of several visions the prophet receives.

The prophet Zechariah speaks here after the return from exile in Babylon, when the people were rebuilding the temple. A little later, the angel explains that the scroll is a curse against theft and false swearing. Its size, about ten by five meters, seems to match that of the holy place of the temple, although scholars interpret this in different ways. It shows that God takes justice seriously.

Today we can examine our honesty: keeping what we promise, not taking what belongs to others, and always telling the truth, even when no one is watching.
exp.8:12:
God says that he uses his people the way a warrior uses his bow. The phrase "bend Judah as My bow" means pulled tight, ready to shoot. Judah is the bow, and Ephraim is fitted to it like an arrow. God promises to rouse the sons of Zion against the sons of Greece, and to make his people like the sword of a mighty man.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah to a people who had returned from exile and felt weak. It comes after the promise of a humble king (9:9-10). Scholars debate which historical event the mention of "Greece" refers to: some think of conflicts from the Greek era, others see a broader or prophetic meaning. There is no complete certainty.

When you feel weak or without strength, remember that victory depends on God, not on you. He takes you in his hands, prepares you, and uses you in his time. Your part is to let yourself be shaped and to trust in him.
exp.2:9:
This verse describes a future time when people will live in peace and good neighborliness. Sitting "under your own vine and fig tree" was an image of tranquility: each person on their own land, without fear, inviting their neighbor to share the shade and rest.

The LORD of Hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah to Joshua the high priest, after the return from exile. God promises to bring his servant, the Branch, which many Christians understand as Christ, and to remove sin from the land in a single day. That cleansing makes way for the peace the verse describes.

For today: where God forgives, he also restores relationships. Invite someone to your table or into your home this week, and be an instrument of peace.
exp.10:2:
Listen to the wailing of the shepherds, because their glory is in ruins. Listen to the roaring of the young lions, because the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed. "Glory" means splendor or greatness. The "thickets of the Jordan" refer to the dense, leafy growth along its banks, where the lions lived.

Zechariah announces a judgment of God using images of a devastated forest, from Lebanon to Bashan and the Jordan. Interpreters disagree about whom the trees, the shepherds, and the lions represent, though they are probably the leaders of the people and their neighboring nations. Next God speaks of the people as sheep mistreated by shepherds without compassion.

For today: what seems great and secure can fall when it turns away from God. Whoever has authority, in the home, the church, or the workplace, must care for others with compassion and not take advantage of them.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that God invites the "prisoners of hope" to return to the stronghold, that is, to a safe place. They are captives who still wait on God. The word for "return" means to come back or go back. "Double" means twice as much: God promises to restore more than what was lost.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah. He announces the coming of a King who brings peace to the nations, and who rescues his people by the blood of his covenant. The dry well is an image of an empty cistern, a symbol of captivity and abandonment. Many Christians see here a prophecy of Christ. The exact way the "double" was fulfilled is understood in several different ways.

For today: if you are going through a season of confinement, weariness, or loss, do not let go of hope. Return to God as your refuge, trusting that he is faithful to his promises, even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.7:5:
God asks: if this promise seems very impossible to the small group that returned from exile, will it also be impossible for him? The implied answer is no. "Impossible" means something that cannot be done, and "the remnant" refers to the people who came back to their land.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zechariah, after the return from Babylon. Jerusalem was weak and only partly rebuilt. God promises that elderly people will sit in its streets and children will play there, a sign of peace and security. For that small community, such a change seemed like a distant dream. Some scholars see a partial fulfillment in that period and others see it also in the future; the Bible does not fully detail it here.

Today, when a situation seems impossible to us, we can bring it honestly to God. Our doubt is real, but it does not limit his power. Let us trust him and keep obeying step by step.
exp.1:2:
This verse tells how the angel who was speaking with Zechariah in the vision went away, and how another angel came forward to meet him. The words "went forth" mean that he was on his way, and "came forward to meet him" means that he approached him in order to speak to him.

Zechariah sees a man with a measuring line, who wants to measure Jerusalem so that it can be rebuilt. Before he can do so, this second angel appears with an urgent message: the city will not need walls, because God himself will protect it like a wall of fire. Who the man with the measuring line is is not made clear in the text, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

God often goes beyond our plans and measurements. Before you shut yourself up in your calculations, seek his direction and trust that his care is greater than any wall you could build.
exp.4:9:
Here Zechariah asks the angel where they are taking the basket. It was a large container used for measuring grain. Inside was a woman called "the Wickedness." Zechariah sees two women with stork-like wings lifting it up between earth and sky, and he wants to know where it is going.

The prophet Zechariah speaks in a night vision, and the angel who speaks with him explains what he sees. God shows that He removes sin from the midst of His people. The answer says they are carrying it to Shinar, or Babylon, a place that in the Bible stands for rebellion against God. The details of the vision are interpreted in several ways.

For today: it is not enough to hide sin; we need to ask God to remove it from our lives. Let us confess it honestly, and trust that He cleanses and restores.
exp.7:7:
It says that God himself will bring his people back to live in Jerusalem. God promises to be their God with faithfulness and uprightness, keeping his word.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah. The people had returned from exile and were rebuilding the temple, but they felt weak and discouraged. God assures them that he will gather his people from the east and the west, and that nothing is impossible for him, even though it may seem difficult to them.

When something seems too hard to you, or you feel far from God, remember that he is faithful to his promises. Trust that he knows how to restore what seems lost, and keep going with your part, like the builders of the temple.
exp.3:3:
Zechariah keeps speaking with the angel who explains his visions. After describing a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees on either side, he asks, "What are these, my lord?"

Zechariah prophesies after the return from exile in Babylon, when the people were rebuilding the temple with little strength and much discouragement. The angel's answer comes right away: the work of Zerubbabel would not be accomplished by human power, but by the Spirit of God. The oil from the olive trees is usually understood as an image of that Spirit, although some details of the vision are interpreted in different ways.

Today we can learn to ask with humility when we do not understand what God is doing. And when we feel few or weak for a task, let us remember that God works by his Spirit, not only by our own strength.
exp.10:3:
God commands the prophet to care for and guide the sheep "marked for slaughter," that is, a people destined to be mistreated and sacrificed. To "pasture" means to shepherd: to nourish, protect, and lead the flock.

The Lord speaks, whom the prophet calls "my God." Just before this, the ruin of powerful leaders is described, likened to cedars and shepherds. The verses that follow show that buyers and sellers exploited the people without remorse, and their shepherds had no compassion. Scholars debate which historical moment is meant, and many Christians see here a shadow of the rejected Good Shepherd. This is interpreted in different ways.

For today: if God places us in charge of others, in the family, the church, or the workplace, we should care for the vulnerable with compassion, and not take advantage of them.
exp.2:6:
God speaks to Joshua, the high priest, and sets a condition: if he walks in God's ways and keeps God's instructions, he will be entrusted with authority in the temple. "You will govern my house" means he will be responsible for directing the temple, and "you will also have charge of my courts" means he will watch over its courtyards. "I will give you a place among these who are standing here" means he will have a place of access among the angels who stand there.

The people have just returned from exile. Joshua appears dirty and accused, but God forgives him and clothes him in clean garments. Now the angel of the Lord reminds him that forgiveness leads to a faithful life and to responsibility.

For today: God cleanses us by grace, but he also invites us to walk with him every day. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience and faithfulness in your work, your family, or your church.
exp.0:17:
Zechariah looks up and sees four horns in a vision. In the Bible, a horn usually stands for strength or power, often of a kingdom or an enemy.

The prophet Zechariah speaks, and God explains the vision through an angel. The people had returned from exile and were discouraged. God has just promised that he will rebuild Jerusalem. The horns are the nations that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. The four have been understood in different ways: as specific empires, or as an image of opposition coming from every direction. There is no single certain interpretation.

For today: when your problems seem bigger than your strength, remember that God sees those threats and keeps fulfilling his promises. Trust in him and keep doing what is yours to do.
exp.0:14:
God says he is fiercely angry with the nations that live in comfort and feel secure. He was only a little angry with his own people, but those nations did not show mercy. Instead, they added to the disaster and made the suffering worse.

The Lord speaks, and the angel asks Zechariah to announce it. This takes place after the exile in Babylon, when the people had returned to Jerusalem and were discouraged. God tells them that he still cares for them with great passion. His discipline had been limited, but others took advantage of it with cruelty.

For today: do not take advantage of another person's pain, and do not stay indifferent when someone is suffering. God sees injustice, even when he seems silent, and he cares for his own. We can help those who are going through trials.
exp.12:5:
Someone asks, "What are these wounds on your chest?" And the person answers that they were received in the house of their friends.

The context is the day when God will clear the land of false prophecy. A false prophet denies being one and tries to hide his wounds, which may have come from his own practice or from punishment by his own family. Many Christians also see here a sign of Christ, wounded by his own people, especially given the next verse about the struck shepherd. Scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: do not hide your truth behind excuses. Be honest with God, and trust that Jesus knows well the pain of being hurt by those who claimed to be friends.
exp.3:10:
In this verse, the prophet Zechariah continues talking with the angel who explains the vision to him. Now he asks about the two olive trees standing on the right and left of the lampstand. The lampstand is a golden lamp with several lights, and the olive trees are the trees from which oil is pressed.

Zechariah speaks here with the angel. God shows him this vision to encourage Zerubbabel and the people who were rebuilding the temple, even though the work seemed small and weak. The olive trees keep supplying oil to the lamp without stopping. Later, the text says they stand for "the two anointed ones" (4:14), and many believe these are Zerubbabel and Joshua, though not everyone sees it the same way.

For today: God sustains his work by his Spirit, not by our strength. If you feel small or tired, ask him to fill you again, and dare to ask him about what you do not understand, as Zechariah did.
exp.5:4:
Zechariah asks the angel what the chariots mean, and the angel tells him that they are "the four spirits of heaven." They go out from their station before the Lord of all the earth, that is, from the place where they wait for his command. The colors of the horses are a matter of description, and the exact meaning of those terms is not certain.

This is the last of Zechariah's eight night visions, given after the return from exile. The angel who explains the visions to the prophet is the one speaking. The chariots are sent by God to travel through the earth. Many understand them to show his authority over the nations, although the word for "spirits" can also be rendered as "winds," and interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: God still governs everything, even when the world seems confused. You can rest in the fact that nothing escapes him, and place yourself at his disposal, ready to go wherever he sends you.
exp.7:11:
This verse promises a new season for the people. The seed will be prosperous, so the sowing will bear a good harvest. The vine will yield its fruit, the ground will yield its produce, and the skies will give their dew, which was an important source of moisture for the crops. God says he will give all of these things to the remnant of this people, those who returned from exile, as their inheritance.

God speaks, through the prophet Zechariah, to the Jews who had returned from Babylon and were rebuilding the temple. Before that there had been poverty, insecurity and conflict among them. Now God promises to change that situation and to encourage them.

For today: even if you have gone through times of scarcity or division, God knows how to restore. Trust in Him, keep sowing with effort, and seek peace with others.
exp.4:3:
God says that he himself will send out the curse, which is the flying scroll. This curse will enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by God's name. It will stay in that house and destroy it completely, right down to its timbers and stones.

The phrase "destroy it" in the verse means the curse wipes out the house entirely. The "timbers" are the wooden beams and boards of the house.

Here the phrase "swears falsely" means making false promises in God's name.

The Lord of hosts speaks through the prophet Zechariah, in a vision. The people had returned from exile, and God wanted a clean and honest people. The scroll shows that God's law reaches everyone, throughout the whole land. Scholars debate details of the message, but the central idea is clear: God judges theft and deceit.

Today we can examine our own honesty: keeping what we promise, not using God's name to back up lies, and returning what does not belong to us.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that the prophet, speaking in God's name, cares for a flock marked for slaughter, especially the afflicted of the flock. He takes two staffs, which are shepherd's staffs. He calls one Favor and the other Union. The phrase "I pastured the flock" means that he tended and fed them.

The prophet Zechariah speaks here, representing God as the shepherd. His people were exploited by cruel leaders who sold them and killed them without remorse. The two staffs are usually understood as God's favor and the unity of the people. Interpreters debate exactly whom this shepherd represents; many Christians see here a shadow of Christ.
