For today: God looks upon the most vulnerable, and we too should do the same. This week, look for a concrete way to accompany or help someone who is suffering, with kindness and without expecting anything in return.
exp.4:6:
In Zechariah's vision, the cover of lead was raised, and there was a woman sitting inside the basket. The basket was a large container used for measuring grain. The lead cover was heavy, so the moment it was lifted was striking to see.

The angel explains the vision to Zechariah, which was seen at night. The woman represents wickedness, and the basket shows how it spread over the whole land. Many understand that God removes sin from his people. The heavy lead cover suggests that the wickedness is kept shut in and cannot escape. The symbolic details are interpreted in different ways.

God does not overlook sin, but he does not leave us tied to it. Today you can ask him to show you what you should let go of, and trust that he has the power to take it away.
exp.0:16:
God commands the prophet to keep proclaiming a message of hope. His cities will overflow with prosperity once again. He also promises that he will again comfort Zion, that is, Jerusalem and its people, and that he will choose Jerusalem. The words "again" and "will" show that God has not finished with them.

The LORD of Hosts speaks through an angel and through the prophet Zechariah. The people had returned from exile in Babylon and were living discouraged, with the city and the temple not yet rebuilt. God says that his anger was brief and that now he returns to Jerusalem with compassion. This verse closes the vision with a promise of restoration.

For today: when everything seems to be in ruins, remember that God continues to comfort and choose his people. Your present situation is not the final word; trust him and keep moving forward with hope.
exp.13:17:
It says that if the people of Egypt do not go up to Jerusalem to worship God at the Feast of Tabernacles, the rain will not fall on them. The word "people" here means a nation. "Plague" is a punishment, and "the nations" are the peoples who are not Israel. Egypt is singled out in a special way, perhaps because it depended on the river Nile more than on rain, so the punishment would stand out. This is a possible explanation, not something certain.

The prophet Zechariah speaks, announcing what God will do "in that day," when the Lord reigns over all the earth. The Feast of Tabernacles recalled God's care in the wilderness and the harvest. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future fulfillment, others a symbolic way of speaking about universal worship of God. In both cases the message is that all nations must acknowledge Him as King.

For today: God deserves our worship and not only our comfort. We can ask ourselves whether we seek Him with consistency or only when we need Him. Today, take a moment to thank Him for what you receive from Him every day.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the angel who was speaking with Zechariah returned and woke him, just as a person is awakened from sleep. The phrase "came back" shows that the angel had already been with him before this moment.

Zechariah records a series of visions he received at night, after the Jews returned from exile, while they were rebuilding the temple. Here it is not an ordinary sleep he is roused from. He seems to have been overwhelmed by what came before, and the angel lifts him up so he can see the new vision, the one of the golden lampstand and the olive trees. Interpreters explain this in different ways, but the text itself gives no further details.

For today: sometimes we need God to awaken our hearts so that we can understand what He wants to show us. We can pray simply: "Lord, open my eyes and give me attention to your Word."
exp.10:5:
God says that he will no longer have compassion on the people of the land. He will cause each man to fall into the hands of his neighbor and of his king, and they will devastate the land. God will not rescue it from their hands.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah. Earlier he had commanded that a mistreated flock be cared for: its buyers killed them without feeling guilty, its sellers grew rich, and its shepherds felt no compassion. This judgment comes because the people and their leaders abused the weak. Scholars debate exactly who the "sheep" and the "king" refer to, so it is wise to read this with humility.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat the vulnerable. Today I can ask myself whether, in my work, my family or my community, I take advantage of others or care for them with justice and compassion.
exp.10:11:
This verse says that the prophet, playing the role of the people's shepherd, asks the owners of the flock for his wages. He gives them a choice: if it seems right to them, they should pay him; if not, they should keep the wages. They weigh out thirty pieces of silver, that is, thirty coins. The phrase "give me my wages" in the verse means "pay me what I am owed."

Zechariah acts as a shepherd sent by God to a people who reject him. That low payment shows how little they valued the shepherd and God himself. According to Exodus 21:32, thirty shekels was the price of a slave. The New Testament connects this passage with the thirty coins of Judas (Matthew 26:15; 27:9-10), although scholars explain that connection in several ways.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we value God and his Word as something precious or only as something cheap and optional. Let us give them first place with gratitude and obedience.
exp.7:15:
What it says: God tells his people what they must do. First, speak the truth to one another, to your neighbor or to whoever is near you. Second, render true and sound judgments in your gates, that is, in the public places of the city where cases were settled. Judgments that are sound aim at justice that brings harmony and restoration, not division.

Context: The words come through the prophet Zechariah to the people who had returned from exile. God reminds them that he had once punished them for the wrongdoing of their ancestors, but now he promises good to Jerusalem. He tells them not to be afraid, and shows them how to live as a restored people.

For today: Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true and helps peace. Be honest at home, at work, and in the church, even when the truth is costly. When you have to give an opinion or make a decision, aim to be fair and to seek reconciliation.
exp.9:5:
God promises to strengthen the house of Judah, the southern kingdom, and to save the house of Joseph, the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim. He says he will restore them because he has compassion on them. Compassion means mercy, and rejected means that God had turned away from them. They will be as though he had never rejected them, because he is the LORD their God and will answer them.

The one speaking is the LORD, through the prophet Zechariah, to a people who had returned from exile and felt weak. First he promises that they will be strong in battle because he will be with them. Then he announces joy, return, and growth in number. Some see here a near fulfillment and others a hope for the future; the Bible does not fully spell this out.

For today: if you feel you have failed or that God has turned away, remember that he is merciful and hears you. You can return to him with confidence and pray to him today.
exp.13:4:
It says that, when the Mount of Olives is split in two, a great valley will form, and the people will flee through it to find safety. It is compared to the flight that took place because of an earthquake in the days of King Uzziah of Judah. In the end, God himself arrives, accompanied by "all the holy ones," a phrase that can refer to his people or to heavenly beings. The name "Azal" appears to be a nearby place, but it is not known with certainty where it was.

The prophet Zechariah speaks on God's behalf to a people who had returned from exile. He announces a final day when God fights for Jerusalem and rescues it. Christians interpret this passage in different ways: some see it as something still in the future, others in a more symbolic way.

For today: even if everything shakes around you, God comes to rescue his own. Today you can trust in him, pray with calm, and remain faithful, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.2:2:
It says that Joshua, the high priest, stood before the angel of the LORD dressed in filthy garments, meaning dirty, stained and unclean. It was clothing unfit for someone who was to serve in the presence of God.

Zechariah describes a vision he received after the return from exile in Babylon. Satan accused Joshua, but God defended him and called him "a brand plucked out of the fire," that is, a stick rescued from the flames. Many understand that the filthy clothes represent the sin of the people and of the priest who represented them. The next verse shows that God himself cleanses him.

Today, when we feel dirty because of our failures or accused by guilt, we can come to God without pretending. He does not leave us in shame: he forgives, cleanses and renews.
exp.2:1:
Here the LORD himself speaks to Satan and says, "The LORD rebukes you, Satan!" It is a firm command for him to be silent. God reminds him that he chose Jerusalem and calls Joshua "a firebrand snatched from the fire," that is, a half-burned stick that someone pulled out of the fire in time. "Rebuke" means to correct with authority, and "Satan" is the one who accuses.

Zechariah sees a courtroom scene. Joshua, the high priest, represents the people who returned from exile in Babylon. Satan stands at his right hand, the place of the accuser, to point out his guilt. Joshua appears in filthy clothes. But God himself defends him, not because he is perfect, but because he rescued him and chose him.

For today: when guilt or accusations crush you, remember that your worth does not depend on your record, but on the grace of God who rescued you. Come before him with confidence, and let him clothe you again.
exp.4:5:
Zechariah sees a vision and asks what it is. The angel answers that it is a measuring basket, a fairly large container for grain, and that it is going forth. He then adds: "This is their iniquity in all the land."

An angel speaks to Zechariah and explains a series of visions. Earlier, God had announced a curse on thieves and on those who swear falsely. Now the measuring basket represents how wrongdoing spreads across the land, and in the verses that follow it will be carried away.

For today: God sees injustice and lies, even when they are hidden. Today we can ask him to help us be honest in small things, such as at work, with money, and in what we promise.
exp.12:7:
It says that throughout the whole land, by the Lord's decision, two thirds of the people will be cut off and perish, and they will be lost. Only one third will be left in that land.

The Lord speaks, and the theme is judgment on his people. The wounded shepherd (v. 7) is understood by many Christians as Jesus, while Jews and other interpreters see him in different ways. The sheep are scattered. But the next verse clarifies the purpose: the remaining third will be refined like silver and gold, until they say, "The Lord is my God." Whether "the land" means only Israel or something broader is interpreted in various ways.

For today: when God allows trials, it is not always to destroy us, but to cleanse us and draw us closer to him. In the midst of pain, we can call on his name with confidence, knowing that he hears us and calls us his own.
exp.8:13:
It says that the LORD himself will appear over his people to defend them. His arrow will go out swiftly, like lightning. The Lord GOD will sound the ram's horn, which was a sign of war or of warning, and will advance in the whirlwinds of the south, that is, the wind from the south, which in that region could be very strong.

The prophet Zechariah speaks to a people who had returned from exile and felt weak. God promises them protection and victory. The mention of Greece has been understood in several ways: some see it in relation to future conflicts for Israel, others in a broader picture of God's struggle against the power of nations. There is no single certain interpretation.

For today: when you feel weak or without a way out, remember that God does not leave you alone. Rest in his care and move forward with hope, trusting that his power is greater than your fears.
exp.1:11:
God says that he will take possession of Judah as his own portion, a precious possession, in the Holy Land. He also says that he will once again choose Jerusalem. The phrase "take possession" means that God will hold Judah as his own, and "once again choose" means that he will select it once more.

Zechariah speaks after the return from exile in Babylon. The people were few and discouraged while they rebuilt. The Lord promises to dwell among them and that many nations will join themselves to him. Some see here a hope that looks beyond that time, toward the Messiah; others read it mainly as applying to that period.

For today: even if you feel small, far away, or of little worth, God can choose you again and care for you. When you fail, do not think that he has forgotten you. Come to him with confidence and let his love encourage you to begin again.
exp.0:5:
God asks whether his words and his statutes, which he gave through the prophets, did not overtake the people's ancestors. His statutes are his decrees and instructions. The answer is yes, they did overtake them: the ancestors did not listen, they suffered the consequences, and in the end they confessed that the LORD of Hosts had dealt with them according to their ways and their deeds. God did what he had warned.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zechariah to the people who had returned from exile in Babylon, in the second year of King Darius. He reminds them that their fathers' disobedience brought punishment, so that they do not repeat the mistake and turn away from God.

Today we can learn that God's words are not empty. Instead of hardening ourselves, we can listen to his Word in time, recognize our errors, and turn back to him with sincerity.
exp.3:11:
Zechariah presses the angel and asks a second time what the two olive branches mean. These branches stand beside two gold pipes from which golden oil pours. The phrase about the branches pouring out oil by themselves means that the oil flows out on its own, without anyone squeezing them.

Zechariah speaks with the angel, who explains a vision: a golden lampstand fed by olive trees. The people were rebuilding the temple and felt weak. The answer that follows speaks of two "sons of oil" standing before the Lord. Many think this refers to Zerubbabel, the governor, and Joshua, the high priest, but this is not certain. Oil often symbolizes the Spirit of God.

For today: God does not ask us to shine by our own strength. He supplies the oil steadily. We can ask him each day for his Spirit and trust that he sustains what he has entrusted to us, even when it seems small.
exp.13:19:
In that coming day that Zechariah describes, even the bells on the horses will bear the words "Holy to the Lord." Those words were once found only on the gold plate worn by the high priest. Moreover, the ordinary pots in God's house will be as holy as the bowls used at the altar, which were set apart most strictly for worship.

Zechariah, a prophet after the exile, speaks of that time, when the Lord will reign over all the earth. Interpreters differ: some understand it as something future and literal, others as a picture of God's kingdom in Christ. Either way, the message is that everyday things will be consecrated.

For today: do not divide your life into the holy and the common. Your work, your meals, and your daily tasks can be done for God. Today, before beginning an ordinary activity, offer it to Him in prayer.
exp.13:20:
On that final day of the Lord, even the ordinary cooking pots in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD of Hosts, just like the vessels used in the temple. Everyone who comes to sacrifice will be able to take pots and use them to cook the meat. The word "Canaanite" refers to a Canaanite, and it has also been understood as "merchant." The verse says that on that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Hosts.

Zechariah is a prophet who speaks after the return from exile. In this chapter he describes the day when the LORD will reign over the whole earth. The idea is that holiness will reach everything, not only what is religious. About the "Canaanite" there are two readings: an impure or foreign person who contaminates worship, or a merchant who takes advantage of the temple to do business. Both point to a temple that is completely clean.

For today: God wants all of our life to belong to him, not only the hour of church. Today you can offer him your work, your home, and your meals, doing each thing with honesty and gratitude.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that the prophet sees a scene like a courtroom. Joshua, the high priest, stands before the angel of the Lord. At his side stands Satan, whose name means "accuser," ready to accuse him. The verse says the angel showed the vision, and the phrase "the high priest" refers to the chief priest. The phrase "at his right hand" was the place of the accuser in a trial.

Zechariah speaks, recounting a vision he received after the return from exile in Babylon. Joshua represents the people and their service in the temple, which was being rebuilt. The verses that follow show that God himself defends and cleanses him. Some see here also an announcement of the forgiveness that God offers to his people.

For today: when you feel accused because of your failures, remember that God is the one who defends you. Bring him your guilt with sincerity and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that God called out to his people and they refused to listen. Later, when they called out in their trouble, God would not listen to them. "Called out" means calling for help or speaking to them. "The LORD of Hosts" is a title that speaks of God as the Lord with all power.

Zechariah speaks to the people who returned from exile in Babylon. God reminds them of what happened to their ancestors: they would not pay attention to the words of the prophets, they hardened their hearts, and punishment came. God shows them the past so that they will not repeat the same mistake and will obey now.

For today: let us not wait until we are in trouble to seek God. Listening to his Word with a willing heart is better than ignoring it. But God always invites us to return to him with sincerity and humility.

sum.2: In a vision, the high priest Joshua appears in filthy clothes while Satan accuses him, but God rebukes Satan. Then God removes his sin, dresses him in clean clothes, and promises that if he remains faithful, he will serve in God's house. God also announces that he will send his servant, the Branch, and remove the sin of the land in a single day.
sum.3: In a vision, Zechariah sees a gold lampstand with seven lamps, fed with oil by two olive trees. The angel explains that Zerubbabel's work, rebuilding the temple, will be accomplished "not by an army, nor by strength, but by my Spirit," and that no one should look down on small beginnings. The two olive trees are the ones who stand before the Lord of all the earth.
sum.7: God promises to return to Jerusalem and live in the middle of it, so that it will be a real city, with elderly people and children playing in its streets. He encourages his people to work without fear, to speak the truth, and to live in justice and peace. Their fasts will become joyful feasts, and people from many nations will come to seek God.
sum.0: God calls his people to return to him and not repeat the mistakes of their ancestors, and he promises to return to them. In a vision of horses among the myrtle trees, God says he is jealous for Jerusalem, that he will rebuild his house and comfort the city. The four craftsmen come to tear down the horns that scattered Judah.
sum.6: In the fourth year of King Darius, some men came to ask whether they should keep weeping and fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for years. God answered that their fasts had really been for themselves. He asked them to practice justice and mercy, and to take care of the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor. Their ancestors refused to listen, and because of this they were scattered and their land was left in ruins.
sum.13: Zechariah announces the day of the LORD: the nations will attack Jerusalem, but God himself will go out to fight, will come with his holy ones, and will be King over the whole earth. Living waters will flow out from Jerusalem, and the peoples will go up to worship him. Everything in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD.
sum.9: God invites his people to ask him for rain, and he condemns the idols and diviners who deceive them and leave them without a shepherd. He will punish the bad shepherds, strengthen Judah and Joseph, and bring them back from distant lands with compassion. In this way they will be able to walk in joy in his name.
sum.12: God promises an open fountain to cleanse Jerusalem from sin and to remove the idols and the false prophets. Then he strikes the shepherd, the sheep are scattered, and the people pass through the fire like silver and gold. In the end, those who remain will call on his name and say, "The LORD is my God."
sum.8: God announces judgment against the neighboring nations, such as Tyre and Philistia, despite their wealth and pride. He then promises Zion a righteous king, humble and victorious, riding on a donkey, who will bring peace and rule from sea to sea. God will deliver and protect His people like a precious flock.
sum.4: Zechariah sees a flying scroll that carries God's curse against thieves and those who swear falsely, and that curse consumes their houses. Then he sees a woman named Wickedness shut inside an ephah with a lead cover, and two winged women carry her off to the land of Shinar to set her down there in a house. The message is that God removes the sin of his people.
sum.10: God announces judgment on the land, and the prophet tends a flock that has been mistreated, but the flock rejects its shepherd. Because of this, he breaks his two staffs, and his wages of thirty pieces of silver are thrown into the house of the LORD. In the end, God warns that he will send a foolish shepherd and will punish the worthless shepherd.
sum.5: Zechariah saw four chariots with horses of different colors coming out from between two mountains of bronze. The angel explained that they were the four winds going out over the earth on behalf of the Lord. Then God commanded that the priest Joshua be crowned, and that the one called the "Branch" be announced: he would build the temple and rule. People from far away would help build it, if they obeyed God.
sum.1: Zechariah sees a man who is going to measure Jerusalem, but God announces that the city will be so large that it will have no walls, because He Himself will be its wall of fire and its glory. He calls His people to leave Babylon, promises to watch over them as the apple of His eye, and says He will come to live among them, and that many nations will join themselves to Him.
sum.11: God promises to protect Jerusalem and Judah when the nations come against them, and the nations will be wounded and confused. In addition, he will pour out on them a spirit of grace and prayer, and they will look on the one they pierced with great mourning, each family grieving separately.
